3 Understanding Blockchain Technology Adoption in Human Resource Management A Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) Approach

Vishal Kumar, Sushil Kumar, Arvind Mewada, and Saaema Akhtar

DOI: 10.1201/9781003545620-5

3.1 Introduction

Blockchain technology, alongside other emerging technologies like artificial intelligence (AI), has significantly transformed various business sectors, including human resource management (HRM) [1]. Blockchain technology is known for decentralised and secure data management capabilities. To reshape processes, improve decision-making, and enhance operational efficiency, it has become integral to modern business operations [2]. Although most of the recent research has generally focused on newly adopted blockchain technologies in different areas, a limited number of studies have specifically looked at the potential of blockchain in HRM. Still, in spite of the parallelism of blockchain and AI, these two progressive technologies are advancing rapidly in this digital era [3]. AI refers to the capabilities through which computers can be taught to perform activities that a human would normally execute, and such a system can also learn from previous data and modify its tasks in accordance with current requirements. The genesis of the concept took place in the 1940s, but since then, it has undergone various stages of development [4]. Blockchain technology is already an innovation, and its progress is very high, especially in areas such as data storage security and managed decentralisation [5]. Better and more efficient decision-making and improvements in business processes have moved HR to be seen as a strategic partner of the organisations rather than simply a support function [6].

According to the use cases presented in this article, blockchain technology is especially useful in HRM workflows for talent management practices, such as recruitment and employee verification, as well as for dealing with sensitive information securely. It offers a trustworthy and transparent peer-to-peer network. As a result, the efficiency of HR activities increases, and incidents of fraud or data leakage are 36prevented [7]. In addition, blockchain has also changed the way organisations manage HR functions in the employees’ lifecycle, ranging from recruitment, onboarding, and performance appraisal to payroll processing [3,8]. Such tendencies are structured alongside the mounting prioritisation of HR practices of reconceptualising processes whereby blockchain is employed to enhance efficiency and simplify processes whilst increasing the accuracy of data.

While there is an enormous capability of blockchain technology application in HRM, there is still a need to increase the level of usage of the technology further. The lack of integration of blockchain into HRM practices is attributed to many organisations or institutions requiring support to do so due to the perceived complexity, security, and compatibility with the existing systems. Moreover, HR practitioners are key agents of organisational change who have a role in integrating technologies in their operational activities, which in this case is blockchain, but do not understand how it can be beneficial or easily implemented in their day-to-day office tasks [9]. Factors stemming from the HR practitioners who are relevant in blockchain adoption are important to utilise this technology to improve HRM and its processes. This research focuses on important factors influencing blockchain adoption in HRM, which are classified within the technology adoption model (TAM) framework. This study examines the views of HR practitioners about the use of blockchain technology and the factors that influence their choices to incorporate blockchain technology in HR systems [10]. In particular, this study seeks to address the following research questions:

  1. Which factors significantly influence the acceptance of blockchain in HRM?
  2. Which HRM tasks can Chinese professionals perform in a more efficient and useful manner?
  3. What influences the levels of complexity, compatibility, security, and privacy in Blockchain acceptance?
  4. What is the appropriate attitude towards the exchange of cryptocurrencies in organisations?

The purpose of this study is to achieve an in-depth appreciation of blockchain integration in HRM by addressing pertinent questions and offering a guideline on the prospects of successful adoption and implementation. It provides recommendations on how to address existing challenges to enhance HR functions, especially in the role of the HRM in the integration of blockchain technology. Billed as game-changers for HRM, blockchain technology improves speed, scalability, and secure data manipulation and may change the relationship of HR to practice in organisations. This chapter discusses some of the issues that affect the diffusion of blockchain and advises HR practitioners and organisations who wish to use blockchain on its advantages.

3.2 Literature Review

3.2.1 Adoption of Blockchain Technology in HRM

The HRM sphere has been revolutionised by blockchain in terms of security, transparency, and efficiency. The system integration has improved the delivery of services in HRM functions with the assurance of data consistency [11]. It is distributed 37and cannot be corrupted, which is very useful in HR for handling sensitive data (employee files, payment records, and documents pertaining to compliance) [12]. Blockchain provides a dependable form of record keeping and accounting, which is consistent with classical methods for maintaining information confidentiality and renders tamper-proof the changing of such information, thus increasing trust and accountability in various HR processes [13].

Because of blockchain, a range of HR activities, such as talent acquisition, contract management, and performance tracking, are impacted [14]. Blockchain reduces operational costs and positions HR as a strategic partner in achieving broader organisational goals by streamlining these processes [15]. As a result, the roles of HR have shifted from administrative support to a key player in driving organisational transformation through secure and efficient data management practices.

3.2.2 Technology Adoption Models in HRM

The adoption of blockchain in HRM has been examined through various theoretical models (the TAM and the technology-organisation environment) [16]. The TAMcomprises constructs such as Perceived Usefulness (PU) and Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU), which are widely used to understand individual and organisational acceptance of new technologies. It focuses on the behavioural aspects of technology adoption as users perceive the ease of use and usefulness of blockchain applications in HR. On the other hand, the technology-organisation environment model incorporates organisational and environmental factors such as top management support, technology readiness, and external influences [17]. Existing research studies that use these models have identified barriers and facilitators of blockchain integration within HR functions, such as perceived complexity, security concerns, and compatibility with existing systems [18]. Even though these insights are valuable afterwards, research gaps must be addressed to understand the factors that influence blockchain adoption in diverse organisational contexts.

3.2.3 Key Determinants: Compatibility, Complexity, Security, and Privacy

Blockchain technology adoption in HRM is influenced by several critical factors, which include compatibility, complexity, security, and privacy concerns. Compatibility means the seamless integration of blockchain with existing HR systems and processes. It indicates that high compatibility is linked to a smoother implementation process and greater acceptance among HR professionals, leading to higher PU of the technology [19]. However, complexity refers to how hard it is to perceive the adoption of blockchain technologies. In this respect, HR professionals find it too complex; in addition, the need for deep training serves as an obstacle to their adoption. Therefore, designing blockchain-based solutions that are user-friendly and easily integrable into daily workflows is critically important.

Moreover, security and privacy issues are paramount because HR data are sensitive. A decentralised structure, along with cryptographic features in blockchain, presents an important basis for effective data integrity and the reduction of the possibility of unauthorised access. Furthermore, addressing these critical points rightly is of vital importance to establish trust in blockchain-based 38HR systems. By treating such key determinants, organisations can promote a healthy environment to adapt blockchain, thereby strengthening HR departments to apply this technology in their departments in a much more effective and secure way than before.

3.3 Conceptual Framework and Hypotheses Development

3.3.1 Technology Adoption Model (TAM) Framework

TAM is the base of most models that are used to understand technology acceptance. Designing the model, Davis [20] originally came up with this model to predict whether a person will accept and use the technology or not. This model bases its argument upon the constructs of PU and PEOU. PU measures the extent to which an individual feels that application use would improve their job performance. Besides, PEOU is the extent to which a person feels that the use of the technology does not require much effort. TAM has been extensively applied in several organisational and institutional settings to explain technology adoption behaviour.

However, to capture the subtleties of blockchain adoption in HRM better, we extend this framework of TAM in this chapter by adding some additional constructs in the form of Relative Advantage, Compatibility, Complexity, and Security/Privacy concerns. The TAM with these extended constructs provides a much more holistic view of technology adoption from organisational and individual perspectives. This makes it suitable for a study on blockchain integration into HRM. It identifies the characteristics of blockchain technology because the decentralised technology is what makes it highly secure. It considers the influence of these attributes on the perceptions of HR professionals and, thus, on their adoption decisions [20].

3.3.2 Proposed Hypotheses and Conceptual Framework

It presents a conceptual model developed based on the eTAM framework, defining determinants of blockchain adoption in HRM. The variables considered for use in the proposed model include Relative Advantage, Compatibility, Complexity, Security/Privacy, and HR Readiness, which influence both PU and PEOU. Finally, this research develops hypotheses, whereby the constructs of PU and PEOU are supposed to influence the overall adoption of blockchain technology within an HR department.

A conceptual diagram for the proposed framework is presented in Figure 3.1, where arrows link through Relative Advantage, Compatibility, Complexity, Security/Privacy, HR Readiness, PEOU, and PU. These variables are applied to explain blockchain adoption in HRM. The arrow represents the hypothesised relationships and influence directions of these variables.

39

3.3.3 Proposed Hypotheses

The following hypotheses are proposed for empirical testing:

  1. H1a: Relative Advantage positively influences Perceived Usefulness (PU).
  2. H1b: Relative Advantage positively influences Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU).
  3. H2a: Compatibility positively influences Perceived Usefulness (PU).
  4. H2b: Compatibility positively influences Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU).
  5. H3a: Complexity negatively influences Perceived Usefulness (PU).
  6. H3b: Complexity negatively influences Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU).
  7. H4a: Security/Privacy concerns negatively influence Perceived Usefulness (PU).
  8. H4b: Security/Privacy concerns negatively influence Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU).
  9. H5: HR Readiness positively influences Perceived Usefulness (PU).
  10. H6: Perceived Usefulness (PU) positively impacts the adoption of blockchain technology in HRM.
  11. 40H7a: Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU) positively influences the adoption of blockchain technology in HRM.
  12. H7b: Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU) positively influences Perceived Usefulness (PU).

This framework describes the technological and organisational contexts, meaning that it is applicable to HR professionals and organisations with an interest in implementing blockchain technology. This study intends to identify primary drivers and barriers towards the use of blockchain in HRM by testing these hypotheses and providing actionable insights for practitioners.

3.3.4 Practical Implications

Other variables in the extended TAM framework could specifically be relevant to blockchain. A richer understanding of the technology adoption process in HRM because it captures and sheds light on aspects such as organisational readiness, security/privacy concerns, and characteristic-type technology as shaping perceptions toward blockchain technology. It is germane to HR professionals and managers to use blockchain to better the HR functions, such as recruitment, payroll management, and employees’ personal data security. However, the key factors discussed will help organisations prepare tailored strategies to eliminate adoption barriers and foster an ideal environment for efficient blockchain implementation in HRM. Thus, the current study contributes to the more general literature on technology adoption by providing insights into how HRM can change due to the integration of emerging technologies.

3.4 Research Methodology

3.4.1 Research Design

The research design defined the methodological approach taken in investigating the adoption of blockchain technology in HRM. This study based its theoretical framework on the TAM and took a two-level analysis, where both organisational and individual levels are considered. A quantitative method was applied to examine how the given factors for adoption, such as relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, security/privacy, and readiness, would impact the adoption of blockchain technology among HRMs. In other words, it is more focused on giving empirical evidence regarding the hypothesised determinants of blockchain adoption in HR practices by structured surveys and statistical analysis.

3.4.2 Sample and Data Collection

Data were collected using the online survey method as it is the most efficient and convenient method for easily reaching the largest number of participants. It targeted HR professionals from various verticals in India to understand their views and experiences regarding using blockchain technology. The sample population consists 41of 120 respondents who are HR managers, executives, and employees engaged in the technology-related functions of HR. Such a sample of diversification makes an understanding of the more general factors that influence the adoption of technology in different organisational contexts possible. 3.4.3 Questionnaire Development and Measurement Scales

A questionnaire was hence created to gather information regarding factors that influence the adoption of blockchain in HRM. The questionnaire consisted of 21 items that were formatted under various constructs based on the review of literature and framework of TAM. Every item was scaled to a rating of 5 points on a Likert Scale, where every respondent agreed or disagreed with the statements ranging between rating “1.”

The importance of the Likert scale is based on the quantification of attitudes and perceptions, which is essential for analysis through mean and other statistical techniques [7]. 3.5.3 Structural Equation Modelling Outcomes

Structural equation modelling (SEM) was employed to examine the relationships between latent variables and to test the proposed hypotheses. The SEM analysis involved two key stages: evaluating the measurement model using confirmatory factor analysis and assessing the structural model to test the path coefficients and hypotheses.

44The SEM path diagram (see Figure 3.2) visualises the relationships between the constructs, indicating both significant and non-significant paths between the variables. The model fit was assessed using several indices, including the standardised root mean residual (SRMR), chi-square, and Normed Fit Index. The results indicated that both the saturated and estimated models exhibited suboptimal fit, with SRMR values exceeding the acceptable threshold, suggesting the need for model refinement. Specifically, the SRMR value was 0.09, above the recommended cutoff of 0.08. The chi-square value was 245.3; the p-value was less than 0.05, and the Normed Fit Index was 0.88, which did not reach a threshold of 0.90.

Several strong relationships were established through the PCs, SEs, and testing of the hypotheses, as shown in Table 3.5. For example, the PC for Relative Advantage and PU was approximately 0.52, with a p-value less than 0.01. This implies that there is a strong support of the hypothesis established. Similar in nature was the case of Relative Advantage and PEOU, for which this study found a PC of 0.45 with a p-value of less than 0.01. Results also showed that security/privacy concerns significantly affect PU along a path coefficient of 0.34 and a p-value of less than 0.05. These path coefficients measure the strength and significance of constructs’ relationships; therefore, they point to important factors influencing the adoption of technology.

3.6 Conclusion

Blockchain technology has become pivotal in transforming HRM. While research on technology adoption in HR is extensive, studies on blockchain’s specific applications in HRM are limited. An industry report outlined the benefits of blockchain in HR, but implementation details remain underexplored. Although various researchers have investigated blockchain deployment strategies and offered qualitative insights, there is a lack of comprehensive empirical studies using established models.

This study aimed to understand factors influencing blockchain adoption in HRM, focusing on HR professionals and key stakeholders. The research framework utilised the TAM, including organisational and individual-level analyses. The proposed model examined five categories: technological, organisational, environmental, “Perceived Usefulness,” and “Perceived Ease of Use.” Data were gathered through an online survey and analysed using partial least squares-structural equation modelling. This analysis provided a complete view of blockchain adoption in HRM, including assessments of reflective models, discriminant validity, and structural models.

4 Blockchain Technology's Key Components, Security Challenges, and Its Evolving Role in Modern Digital Infrastructure

N. Sharmila Banu, K. Deepa, and Mastan Vali Shaik

DOI: 10.1201/9781003545620-6

4.1 Introduction

Blockchain technology was introduced in 2008, and the distributed database was used to track Bitcoin transactions. The successful mining of the genesis block by Nakamoto in 2009 validated the concept of blockchain [1]. The framework concept included the electronic currency system, which is based on a peer-to-peer network, blockchain technology, encoding and timestamps [2]. Peers can successfully transfer values through transactions, negating the necessity for central control to safeguard client privacy and stop identity intruders [3]. From its initiation, from the first crypto-currency to the present blockchain-related approaches for industry 5.0, blockchain technology has been implemented into the communications of several organizations that require precision, probity, and consistency [4, 5, 6].

Nevertheless, the widespread adoption and continuous advancement of new technologies introduce inherent risks and raise concerns regarding blockchain technology. A smart contract is a code snippet made publicly accessible on the Ethereum network [7]. The bitcoin cryptocurrency sustained to gain significance and reputation in 2013, despite Satoshi Nakamoto’s disappearance from medium, code contributions, and papers in 2011. The primary factor contributing to this increase in popularity was the currency’s acceptance by websites and fund-based startups. The technology underpinning Bitcoin is constantly evolving, and human errors and varying standards can influence its implementation. Cryptocurrencies represent the pioneering and most widely acknowledged use of blockchain technology, with Bitcoin standing out as the most prominent instance. They leverage blockchain as a decentralized public ledger to document all transactions, successfully addressing the double spending issue 48linked to digital currency. This framework enables secure and transparent transactions, eliminating the necessity for a trusted intermediary [8].

Rather, there is a blockchain database accessible via the dispersed computer network. Each computer connected to the network is referred to as a node, and each node is given a duplicate copy of the blockchain, which is downloaded automatically. Digital signatures for transactions are created using public key cryptography, which employs two keys, of which there are two types: public and private. There is a mathematical relationship between these two keys. The transactions are more difficult to crack because it is nearly impossible to predict these keys due to the intricacy of the math involved.

A message to be delivered is signed and encrypted using the public key, which may be decrypted by the intended receiver using their private key. Data about every new transaction is distributed to every node in the blockchain database to keep it updated and functioning as a “Worldwide Ledger.” Blockchain technology has been utilized in numerous sectors owing to its distinctive characteristics, including decentralization, security, and transparency. In the healthcare sector, it can enhance patient identity management by offering a reliable and standardized identity for every individual. Its application in information systems facilitates secure data sharing and storage.

Furthermore, incorporating blockchain into wireless networks can bolster security and data integrity, proving an essential resource for managing network assets and user information. In addition, blockchain delivers high-security standards for Internet of Things applications, protecting against unauthorized data access [9,10]. Blockchain technology has considerable potential for transforming electronic health records by improving security, facilitating interoperability, and empowering patients, all while tackling several challenges within the healthcare system [11].

4.2 Components of Blockchain Technology

4.2.1 Decentralization

Decentralization is the progression by which responsibilities and abilities are transmitted from a unified control to each participating body. Blockchain technology prevents the possibility of centralized control, even though each blockchain user or miner accepts a copy of the transaction database. When the miners validate the transaction, a new block is added. The network functions on a peer-to-peer basis in a decentralized setting. This blockchain feature is one of the key components researchers use to construct the Ethereum virtual currency.

4.2.2 Consensus Building

The integrity of data stored on the blockchain is upheld, in part, by the consensus model. However, when the consensus system malfunctions, a range of issues can emerge, such as blockchain connectivity problems, identity failures, authority discrepancies, node verification challenges, and inadequate network representation [12,13]. The efficiency and applicability of a consensus protocol depend on three 49key characteristics: security, activeness, and fault tolerance. Security ensures that the protocol is both compatible and safe, with every node generating outcomes that align with the protocol’s guidelines and are legitimate. Activeness requires that non-value nodes remain operational to ensure that the consensus process can generate a value. Lastly, fault tolerance allows the protocol to recover even if a node involved in the consensus process ceases to function. These characteristics are crucial for maintaining the stability and reliability of blockchain systems.

4.2.3 Transparent

Ten-minute intervals of transactions are adapted by the blockchain network, which periodically self-audits the ecology of a digital asset by checking in with itself every 10 minutes. The grouping of all these communications is termed a block. Precision and the impossibility of corruption are the two qualities that emerge. The utilization of blockchain technology has the potential to enhance the security, efficiency, and transparency of digital transactions. Such advancements can motivate economic growth and promote the greatest trust in digital systems [14].

4.2.4 Open Source

Users of closed-source, decentralized applications must have faith that the data are not accessible from a central source and that the program is decentralized. Closed-source applications prevent people from adopting them. When an application is meant to collect, keep, or transfer user dues, operating on a closed-source network is obviously disgusting. Consumers prefer open-source participation even if it is feasible to develop a closed-source decentralized program. This is because the complexity involved in achieving the expected outcome would be fatal. An open-sourced, decentralized application modifies based on how corporate operations are organized, which was previously dependent on the net as a unifying factor.

4.2.5 Identity and Access

Three primary factors determine a blockchain’s uniqueness and convenience: grouping, private, public and both. Users are not allowed to validate block transactions or write digital agreements on a private blockchain. The classic business and governance concepts are suitable [15]. Public blockchains are made to eliminate intermediaries from transactions while maintaining security. Anyone with internet access can join a public blockchain network by generating smart contracts and participating in block verifications. Grouping blockchains enables a small number of predetermined nodes to have total control and are partially private. It serves as a stand-in for letting any arbitrary person with an internet connection confirm transactions. Platforms such as private blockchains offer transaction efficiency and secrecy. The selection of a blockchain platform is important in digital settings as Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Hyperledger Fabric each provide distinct advantages that address various requirements related to data integrity and security [14].

50

4.2.6 Autonomy

The primary goal of blockchain technology is to transfer confidence from individual, centralized control to the entire group, which lacks any intervention. Information can be safely updated and sent between any nodes in the blockchain system. An association that abides by a group of predetermined systems approved and executes when the requirements are met is known as a smart contract; it is referred to as a decentralized autonomous organization, which is also known as a decentralized autonomous corporation. In blockchain, blocks accumulate the transaction record and the specifics of the smart contract.

4.2.7 Immutability

It is described as data that does not change throughout time. In the context of blockchain, unchanged data with regard to information contained in the block is crucial. This framework guarantees that once information is entered into a block, it cannot be modified without altering all subsequent blocks. This immutability characteristic is a fundamental aspect of blockchain technology, ensuring the integrity and reliability of the system [16]. The recipient of the data is confident in its accuracy and integrity. The immutable nature of blockchain is particularly beneficial for databases involved in financial transactions, as entries are preserved and cannot be altered unless an individual gains control over the nodes of the network.

4.2.8 Anonymity

This part only needs a miner’s blockchain address; no additional information is needed; hence, anonymity helps to resolve trust concerns. This concept utilizes a group of entities that is impossible to differentiate. The sender and recipient sets are the two categories into which the confidentiality set can be separated among them. The components of blockchain technology are illustrated in Figure 4.1.

4.3 Working Process of Blockchain

Blockchain is a publicly accessible ledger that operates through several key processes, outlined below and illustrated in Figure 4.2. First, a node or user broadcasts data to the network, initiating the transaction. Next, the receiving node verifies that the data transmitted over the network is authentic. Once validated, the data are saved to a block. The block is then subjected to proof of work, a process that requires validation by all nodes or clients within the network to ensure the authenticity of the operation. Finally, a consensus mechanism is applied to the validated data, after which the block is added to the blockchain.

4.4 Issues and Challenges in Blockchain Technology

Conquering all the challenges and tackling the issues affecting the contemporary world takes time. The blockchain is used in this situation. It will take time to overcome all the hurdles despite many possibilities. Adopting blockchain is very 51effective, but there is a chance of facing a lot of complexity that influences developers and users. The issues and challenges in blockchain technology are described with the following points:

4.4.1 Scalability

Although transactions per second are a popular measure of blockchain execution scalability, Transaction Processing System (TPS) refers to the number of computations per second because transaction costs and complexity can fluctuate. A network can handle more computations at any given time as more transactions pass [17]. The primary challenge in scaling the execution layer is achieving higher computation rates per second without significantly raising the hardware specifications on each complete node that verifies a block of transactions. As transaction volumes rise, the ability of the blockchain to process these transactions effectively may become a restrictive factor. This concern is especially pertinent for startups that could undergo swift expansion and need a system capable of managing increased demand while maintaining optimal performance [18].

52

4.4.2 Data Protection

The major complication to extensive acceptance is the lack of assurance among blockchain service contributors. There are two aspects related to this concern: organizations might not have confidence based on the security provided by the technology and other users in a network. Every transaction is thought to be secure, confidential, and validated. This is accurate despite the lack of control over approving and authenticating the transactions due to the decentralized nature of the network. An essential element of every blockchain network is the consensus approaches that assist universal concurrence over the present situation of the distributed database across the whole network. Business leaders have discovered that users are more confident in private blockchains without recognized providers. Blockchain introduces the danger of privacy leaking and guarantees open and transparent transactions. Using techniques such as clustering analysis, attackers can successfully deduce the genuine identity of blockchain users.

53

4.4.3 Privacy

Blockchain was intended to be shared with the community. This implies that everyone can view the information added to the blockchain. The supplementary particulars of a transaction are visible, even though the data are unknown when blockchain directory addresses are used as identifiers. Private blockchains limit who can interpret transactions and participate as a node. Though it has weaknesses, a private blockchain is a method for a corporation to use blockchain technology without worrying about disclosing any information to the public.

A private blockchain is not fully decentralized because it contains a governing body that decides the participation of the nodes. This may cause people to have less faith in a blockchain-based result. The transparency of public blockchains can result in privacy challenges, as sensitive information might be accessible to all network participants. This creates significant risks for sectors that manage confidential data, including healthcare and finance [19].

4.4.4 Selfish Mining

Selfish mining is a hidden method used by a few users of distributed digital database systems or blockchain networks to commit fraud. They accomplish this by covertly mining and preserving a block. These miners then reveal their hidden chains to the public when they are longer than the actual ones, and the blockchain system chooses the longest chain as the genuine chain. Blockchain technology provides potential solutions for enhancing data security; however, it also introduces various security challenges that must be tackled to guarantee its successful application in healthcare and other industries [20]. Few security attacks affect the transaction, and the user’s confidence is as follows:

  1. Mitigating 51% Attack Risks: The main function of miners is to validate the transaction request and data so they can investigate the following block even more. Because a 51% attack has the potential to change the entire blockchain, it is perhaps the riskiest in the blockchain sector. This kind of attack is more likely to occur in the chain when there are not enough miners. To prevent 51% assaults, raise the hash rate, enhance mining pool supervision, and avoid providing proof for the task [20].
  2. Sybil Attack: In this attack, hackers fabricate bogus network nodes and overwhelm the indented network with fictitious identities, causing a system meltdown and disturbing chain transactions. The proper utilization of consensus techniques should be considered to prevent the attack. Keep track of all the other nodes and concentrate on the nodes that are only forwarding blocks from the individual to prevent Sybil attacks.
  3. Phishing Attacks: This type of attack is widely increasing nowadays and resulting in actual problems. The main aim of a phishing attack is to hack the user’s credentials by the intruders. They are able to send the administrator emails that appear authentic and collect the qualification details and other related data. At the same time, the user submits their login information 54through a joined bogus hyperlink. Installing trustworthy anti-malware software or malicious link detection software and maintaining systems and software updates will improve the security of the browser and device. Ignore clicking on unidentified links and turning on Wi-Fi while doing online transactions to guard against phishing attempts, especially when utilizing an electronic wallet or other sensitive data.
  4. Routing Attacks: This is a major security issue that should be considered seriously, followed by privacy issues. Hackers can utilize the identity of an account to seize information submitted to internet service providers. There is a chance for intruders to hack the sensitive data or assets without the knowledge of the owners. Users should ensure safe routing mechanisms are implemented with digital signatures, encode owner data, use strong passwords, modify them frequently, and tutor themselves regarding the hazards associated with data security to avoid outing attacks.
  5. Private Key Security Attacks: Blockchain technology is based on the concept of asymmetric key cryptography. Security issues arise when the key is not utilized properly, and the implementation process is not done perfectly. There is a chance of acquiring the private key from the user’s public key.
  6. Blockchain Endpoint Vulnerabilities: The sensitivity of blockchain endpoints is one of the serious concerns in blockchain technology, where hackers can obtain the users’ passwords, keep track of their activities, and aim at the devices. To be safe, the user should regularly monitor the system, time, and location and change the password by providing a strong password and access to the device.

4.5 Conclusion

Blockchain technology is extremely accepted and reviewed due to its disseminated communications and end-to-end quality. This distinctiveness has the potential to maintain various criteria in numerous contexts and uses. With the rapid development and improvement of blockchain, we believe that it will rapidly turn into a very frequent and recognized circumstance. Blockchain can be compared with the internet a few decades ago to a certain extent. Since the core of blockchains is secure and supportive, progressively, the transactions that require security and non-redundancy will consider this expertise. Blockchain technology is expected to become the standard as it matures, even though certain limits currently make many creative applications challenging to implement.

5 Security Mechanisms and Challenges in Blockchain Technology A Comprehensive Framework for Addressing Threats and Enhancing Integrity

J. S. Prasath and Mohd Sameen Chishti

DOI: 10.1201/9781003545620-7

5.1 Introduction

Blockchain technology has become more popular and rapidly growing in recent years. Blockchain networks and blockchain technology are used in various industries, including cyber-security, information and communication technology, finance and banking, energy and infrastructure, entertainment, transportation, supply chain management, insurance, and healthcare technology. Blockchain technology gathers and stores information in groupings known as blocks, and each block can be used to grasp a set abstraction of data. The hybrid privacy-preserving access control scheme is proposed for blockchain with confidentiality considerations [1]. A prototype system confirms its feasibility and effectiveness, achieving low network latency, efficient encryption, and robust data security. The scope, concerns, and potential solutions related to the segregation of blockchain technology and the IoT are addressed [2]. A secure data management scheme that utilizes encryption, integrity verification, and an integrated communication network has been developed [3]. The security and privacy of blockchain are enhanced by fully homomorphic encryption. The blockchain-based Intrusion Detection System is proposed to enhance the Internet of Things (IoT) network security [4]. The machine learning algorithms detect Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks. The protocol to ensure security over the permissioned blockchains is presented [5].

The blockchain mechanism is utilized to maintain the stored information and improve the security level of the protocol. Blockchain is a type of database technology configured to provide a secure and unalterable record of transactions. A secure blockchain-enabled vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication system is projected to 58improve the security of vehicles and secure data sharing and communication among vehicles [6]. These algorithms can certify users, identify illegitimate access, and constitute secure vehicle communication. When a block is filled with data, it is chained to the previous full block, producing a data chain. The data is organized into blocks, each containing a packet of transactions. A novel security mechanism based on ledger technology is proposed [7].

Blockchain technology operates on both public and private networks. Any party may gather the information on public networks, which are internet-based communications, to authorize transactions. The privacy mechanism is achieved through machine learning [8]. Private blockchain networks allow only the authorized enterprise to access the data. Organizations should form the members and provide rights and permissions to access the information related to the transactions. A novel flexible network infrastructure for smart cities is formulated that integrates software-defined networks and blockchain technology [9].

The software-defined networks will identify the possible attacks and send the secured data to the blockchain. A blockchain operates on a distributed network of nodes. This makes it incredibly difficult for intruders who want to purposely collapse the network or manipulate the essential information of an organization. The problems related to real-time big data storage and security concerns are addressed [10].

The blockchain secures and validates transactions using intelligent mathematical algorithms. It is impossible to alter the data since each transaction is encrypted and connected to the previous one. The security in cloud computing is accomplished through an authentication mechanism [11]. The major security goals are confidentiality, integrity (ensuring the accuracy and reliability of information), and availability (making data accessible to authorized parties). The complexity is to achieve a higher level by considering several security goals. The authorization mechanism is proposed based on an association blockchain for internet-enabled equipment [12].

Blockchain technology is specially designed to achieve data integrity. Blockchain technology provides a guaranteed mode to track the motion of products between two places, which might improve supply chain management. A regulated blockchain and a secure and automated key refreshment scheme for IoT devices are proposed [13].

This proposed scheme permits users to validate the originality of the security keys and launch trust in an IoT system. The key management scheme is proposed based on blockchain for usage in internet-enabled devices [14]. The challenges and trends towards blockchain security are proposed [15]. The risk analysis, risk categories, and real-time attacks of blockchain are addressed. The blockchain-based information sharing between devices is discussed [16]. It is designed for usage on internet-enabled devices.

A public blockchain network does not require authentication, allowing everyone to access the information. All blockchain users have identical rights to read, edit, and authorize the blockchain. The participants can access and validate the transactions being processed on the public blockchain. The blockchain mechanism is proposed for internet-enabled equipment [17]. This proposed scheme permits the storage of copious amounts of information. The issues in secure communication of patient information are addressed [18]. The blockchain-based authentication mechanism is projected to meet the security challenges [19].

59Improvements in various security schemes based on blockchain are proposed [20]. The security and privacy-preserving mechanism is proposed based on blockchain technology [21]. The concept of blockchain and its related components are addressed [22]. The solutions for improving blockchain security are also discussed. The blockchain mechanism for intelligent internet-enabled devices is proposed [23].

The solution for protecting the information is addressed. Private blockchains, also called managed blockchains, can be controlled by a single organization. Private blockchains do not provide access to all users, and only authorized parties are allowed to access the networks. The various problems in securing the internet-enabled blockchain technology are discussed [24]. The combination of the internet and blockchain technology is analysed, along with the research issues and trends in blockchain applications [25]. The security challenges, vulnerabilities, attacks, and potential research of smart contracts in IoT are addressed [26]. This work also discusses the potential applications of smart contracts. The blockchain-based technique for identifying the illegitimate node is addressed [27].

The contributions of blockchain for managing wireless sensor network security are discussed. Hybrid blockchains incorporate data from both private and public connections. Industries can set up private, permission-based systems along with public networks. The authorized parties only access the confidential information, whereas the rest of the information is made public access. Hybrid blockchains can provide public access to digital currency while keeping bank-owned currency private. The problems involved in securing Bitcoin are addressed [28].

Every device in a network is enabled to vote for the slave device through a consensus scheme [29]. The architecture of blockchains, security concerns, and certainty problems are addressed [30]. Blockchain can act against data tampering and allows a larger amount of data to be shared among networks. Consortium blockchains are widely used in banking, finance, logistics, healthcare, and insurance. The data communication security for internet-enabled devices is proposed [31]. The blockchain-based security framework is proposed [32].

This security mechanism prevents attacks during data communication. The core security challenges of blockchain technology include vulnerabilities of smart contracts, Sybil attacks, management of private keys, internal attacks, and DDoS attacks. Sybil attacks can be identified and prevented by incorporating reputation-based systems and proof-of-stake schemes. Private key management can be attained through multi-factor authentication, providing an additional security layer. Internal attacks in blockchain can be overcome by utilizing strong encryption methods such as AES-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard), secure routing protocols, strengthening access control mechanisms, and monitoring malicious activity. DDoS attacks in blockchain can be rectified by creating secure smart contracts, incorporating application firewalls, and monitoring the network traffic.

5.2 Security Challenges in Blockchain

The major challenge in the design of blockchain is to accomplish data integrity. The cyber security threats associated with public blockchain are confidentiality and availability. Data integrity can have its threats associated with the source and quality 60of the registered data. The challenges in securing blockchain technologies are lack of regulation, Interoperability, and improper management of private keys.

5.2.1 Lack of Regulation

The growth towards legislation is continuing, as blockchain technology is still relatively new. The lack of regulations in blockchain transactions makes it easier for intruders to utilize weaknesses without issues. The lack of regulation issue can be rectified with the support of blockchain creators, enterprise leaders, and officials. They can serve jointly to make a stable regulation that protects users while promoting innovation. It is essential to create standards and best practices among Blockchain consumers.

5.2.2 Interoperability

The different standards and protocols utilized by blockchain technology. The possibility of security threats occurs during the transmission of data across various blockchains due to the limitations of interoperability. Interoperability issues can be overcome by creating flexible blockchain solutions. The cross-chain bridge mechanism can be utilized to solve the interoperability problem. This cross-chain bridge allows blockchain networks to interact with isolated blockchains to assist data communication.

5.2.3 Poor Management of Private Keys

The private keys must be kept confidential in blockchain technology to protect against unauthorized access to their digital assets. Most users are unaware of the best methods for managing private keys and could intentionally disclose their keys to intruders. The solution for effectively managing private keys is to utilize biometric-based digital signatures. The consumer’s biometric details are used to generate a secret key every time and directly remove it from memory. The best practices that need to be followed for private key management are utilizing strong cryptographic algorithms, secure key generation mechanisms, and storing encrypted keys in separate cryptographic modules.

5.3 Security Threats in Blockchain

Blockchain is related to Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies, and it is widely used in manufacturing sectors, supply chain management, mining, agriculture, energy, and healthcare. Cryptography is used to secure transactions across blockchain networks. The security against cyber-attacks is difficult because of decentralization. The various security threats in blockchain networks are shown in Figure 5.1. The various security threats of blockchain networks are mining threats, network threats and smart contract threats.

5.3.1 Mining Threats

Mining is the operation where devices in the blockchain system authorize and approve transactions. Mining threats include cryptojacking, selfish mining, security vulnerabilities, and resource depletion. In resource depletion, malicious crypto miners can 61utilize a system’s computational power without the consumer’s knowledge, which leads to system slowdowns and high power consumption. Miners get recently minted tokens in return for their computational attempt. Crypto mining malware has been identified as one that can bypass antivirus programs. There is no security mechanism against illegitimate crypto mining. The links may be in the spam mail, infecting websites with crypto-mining droppers. A managed spam filter service can differentiate spam emails from normal ones.

5.3.2 Network Attacks

  • DDoS Attack: A DDoS attack disturbs the data transmission to the end system, and the attackers prevent the end devices from being unavailable to authorized users. A DDoS attack is overly complex to identify due to the difficulties in distinguishing between authorized and malicious requests.
  • Sybil Attack: A Sybil attack is a vicious crime performed to control a blockchain network by generating several false identities to trick network users. The objective is to gain more power in the network and undermine its 62authority. The Sybil attacks can be prevented by selecting the accurate and most appropriate consensus algorithm for the blockchain network and monitoring other nodes that send blocks from individual users.
  • Routing Attack: Routing attacks are related to blockchain network security where malicious activities occur, and the objective is to interrupt the routing of data packets across the internet. An intruder can separate a network into two or more distinct components using routing attacks. Routing attacks can be rectified by implementing powerful encryption before transmitting data, using secure routing protocols, and creating awareness about threats.

5.3.3 Smart Contract Threats

Smart contracts are system codes saved on a blockchain network and can be compiled when conditions are satisfied. Intruders try to insert malicious code into a smart contract, which results in unexpected and unwanted behaviour in the contract. Security must be the highest priority when designing and developing a smart contract. The harshness of security vulnerabilities to smart contracts is apparent in the number of losses in smart contract hacks. Smart contract vulnerabilities pose a major risk to blockchain ecosystems and digital assets. These attacks can be prevented by implementing secure software development practices throughout the contract’s lifecycle and setting up monitoring tools to detect the contracting activity and receive alerts for any abnormal behaviour.

5.4 Security Mechanisms of Blockchain Technology

The major concern in blockchain networks is sharing data and transactions. The various security requirements of blockchain networks are authentication, access control, and confidentiality.

  1. Authentication: Authentication in blockchain is an essential security mechanism for identifying and verifying users online. The hashing process ensures that the data has not been tampered with, verifying the authenticity of the transaction. Cryptographic keys and digital signatures are utilized in blockchain to authenticate users, devices, and systems and prevent identity theft and fraud. Routing protocols authenticate the route, allowing some data before another router receives its routing updates.
  2. Access Control: Access control is a mechanism for distributing rights to the parties to gather data and resources. Access control is related to choosing the permitted actions of authorized participants and arbitrating each effort by a user to access the data in the device. The objective of access control is to prevent the system resources from unauthorized user access.
  3. Digital Signature: The digital signature validates blockchain network transactions, specifically to authenticate transactions. When users perform 63transactions, they must confirm to every node in the system that they are authorized to pay those amounts while preventing other users from spending them.
  4. Key Management: Key management is an essential part of cryptography in dealing with security services, including confidentiality of transactions, authentication, and data integrity. The private keys of authorized parties can be securely stored to avoid leakage and stealing in blockchain networks. Two conventional techniques to realize public key infrastructure are centralized by a certificate authority and decentralized by a web of trust.

  5. Data Privacy: Data privacy in the blockchain is a major concern, and all parties on the network may access any personal or sensitive messages recorded. Data privacy concerns should be addressed to guarantee and protect the user’s confidential information from unauthorized access to blockchain networks. Smart contracts can be susceptible to security threats and misuse, which results in the leakage of sensitive information stored on the blockchain. The distributed characteristics of blockchain act against data breaches and other security vulnerabilities. Zero-knowledge proof is an immense approach to defend data privacy in a blockchain system. In this technique, a person can confirm to others that a given declaration is true without revealing any further information. Different consensus mechanisms are used in blockchain technology. Proof of Work (PoW) eliminates the need for a central authority like a bank, business, or government to monitor and supervise transactions and their corresponding accounts. The PoW algorithm verifies thousands of transactions to ensure the total history of transactions remains perfect and not modified.

    Proof of activity guarantees that all transactions on the blockchain are legitimate and that all miners arrive at a consensus. When the block is mined, authorities with stakes validate and sign the block. Proof of authority is a consensus scheme that allows fast transactions using identity and money as stakes at the cost of decentralization. Proof of Authority influences the value of identities in a private network. The proof of burn algorithm can provide network security as it becomes severe for attackers. When the participants burn more coins, they have more opportunities to mine the next block, which increases the number of awards. Proof of Elapsed Time is a consensus algorithm in a permissioned blockchain network to choose mining rights and the next block miner. The proof of elapsed time algorithm selects who receives to mine coins and who wins a block using an arbitrarily generated amount of time.

5.5 Decentralization

Decentralization in blockchain distributes the rights, control, and decision-making power among several users within a blockchain network. It guarantees that an individual, group, or government does not manage the blockchain. Blockchain provides an efficient way to serve unidentified parties without trusting each other.

64

5.6 Consensus Mechanisms

Consensus mechanisms provide a set of rules and protocols that manage how agreement is reached and how transactions are legalized within the network. The consensus mechanism keeps the blockchain’s security through data maintenance.

5.7 Node Security

A blockchain node is a system that together compiles the blockchain’s software. It facilitates the blockchain in legalizing transactions and maintaining the network’s security by ensuring it remains decentralized. In order to avoid these attacks, it is essential to safeguard the node by creating strong security strategies, such as encryption, firewalls, and secure hosting environments.

5.8 Smart Contracts

It serves similarly to the conventional contract while also automatically enforcing the contract. Smart contracts are programs that compute precisely as their designers program them. Smart contracts can also be used to accomplish complicated corporate practices. A smart contract may automate the tracking of products from the producer to the customer in supply chain management. The smart contract revises the ledger each time the products are exchanged, assuring that everyone in the supply chain has the right to identical information. Digital identity authentication may also be achieved with smart contracts.

5.9 Endpoint Security

The participants of blockchain networks can directly access the network’s endpoint on electronic devices such as computers and mobile phones. Intruders target the end systems, hack critical information, and make the resources unavailable to authorized parties. The endpoint security solution examines and secures each operational endpoint in a network. This is attained through a centralized management console installed on the corporate network or server. These endpoint security tools provide features such as susceptible endpoint detection, multi-factor authentication, real-time monitoring, user behavioural analysis, and others to identify advanced security threats.

5.10 Cryptographic Keys

Cryptography is a technique for protecting data against unauthorized access. The transactions between two nodes in the blockchain are secured using cryptography. The data transmitted across the peer-to-peer networks is encrypted, and hashing is utilized to secure block messages and connect blocks in the blockchain. Blockchain utilizes asymmetric cryptography to secure all transactions stored in the block. Cryptographic keys are essential for operations that take place in blockchain networks. It is necessary to create, utilize, and store the secure key in the blockchain 65technology. Public-key cryptography is a security mechanism that provides digital authentication to the participants. Any user can decrypt coded information transmitted to them and create a digital signature from it for authentication. A public key is open for the network, which others use to validate a transaction and encrypt a message. Authentication is another security mechanism for system login, bank account transactions, and blockchain network security. Authentication protocols make use of cryptography to validate the participant’s identification. The storage and evaluation of electronic signatures is accomplished through cryptography.

5.11 Key Establishment for Bitcoin

Bitcoin is identical to the account where the currency is maintained. The owner should have a private key to utilize the currency. Intruders can hack into the Bitcoin currency through physical or side-channel attacks. An efficient key management scheme is necessary to safeguard the Bitcoin wallet.

  • Password-Based Wallet: The private keys can be preserved by users who create a password. Bitcoin software only provides access to the stored keys when the right password is supplied. Intruders try to steal private keys through brute force attacks. When users forget the password, they cannot access their Bitcoin wallet.
  • Hosted Wallet: Users can access the services of the Bitcoin wallet through a web authentication mechanism. The third party controls the wallet security, and it is suggested to the user that a smaller amount should be maintained in the wallet.

5.12 Future Research

The drawback of blockchain technology is that transactions are overly expensive since most blockchain networks utilize PoW and proof of stake. Federated learning should enhance data privacy and communication security of local devices. Scalable federated learning can deal with multiple devices and handle large data sets. Federated learning may also speed up blockchain application development, enhance blockchain security and performance, and facilitate new artificial intelligence fusion applications.

5.13 Conclusion

This proposed work provides a detailed analysis of security challenges, security threats, and various security mechanisms of blockchain technology. The various security mechanisms of blockchain are addressed. The various consensus mechanisms are discussed in this work, and their performance parameters are compared. This work also discussed the use of cryptographic keys in securing blockchain networks and the key management of the Bitcoin wallet. Finally, the challenges and future research of blockchain technology are discussed. Blockchain enhances information security, transparency, trust, and traceability across business networks. 66Blockchain security built it to become a popular technology for several applications such as data storage, supply chain management, and financial transactions. Future research on blockchain security will involve the implementation of quantum-resistant consensus algorithms. Blockchain security can be strengthened through various quantum-resistant cryptographic algorithms such as code-based cryptography, lattice-based cryptography, hash-based cryptography, and multivariate cryptography. The quantum-resistant algorithm will soon play a key role in blockchain security.

6 The Transformative Impact of Blockchain Technology on the Financial Sector

Shyam Sunder Agrawal, Saloni Raheja, and Amanjot Singh Syan

DOI: 10.1201/9781003545620-9

6.1 Introduction

Blockchain technology is a revolutionary innovation in the digital domain, a decentralised and extremely secure method for relocating and recording data. A blockchain is a decentralised system that accomplishes a continuously mounting collection of data, organised into blocks that are linked and secured through encryption [1, 2, 3]. This decentralised structure eradicates the risk of a single point of failure, as the record is replicated and preserved by all participants in the network. In addition, the cryptographic methodsthat link the blocks make altering the data almost impossible, as the network would directly detect and reject any such attempt. The secure and decentralised countryside of blockchain has significant implications across multiple industries, including finance, supply chain management, and digital identity management. In the financial sector, blockchain technology has great promise for enabling faster, more efficient, and highly transparent transactions. It can also improve supply chain traceability, transparency, and efficiency by tracking goods and commodities in real-time [4].

Furthermore, blockchain-based digital identity solutions provide individuals better regulators over their data, ensuring confidentiality and security [5]. Blockchain differs from traditional centralised systems in that it operates on a decentralised, distributed ledger where transactions are recorded transparently and securely [6]. Blockchain technology confirms and records the transactions using a public ledger without the need for any third-party oversight or control [7]. The system arranges unified blocks in chronological order, each containing a hash of the previous block, which safeguards data integrity and makes the system resistant to meddling. Therefore, the most noteworthy application of blockchain in finance is its potential to convert the primary financial market. The traditional financial market infrastructure has long-faced challenges, but presenting blockchain technology proposals is a promising solution [4][8, 9, 10]. Its decentralised nature and improved security features can 72address problems such as incompetent data management, absence of transparency, and reliance on trusted intermediaries [11].

6.1.1 Financial Services Blockchain Technology Challenges and Benefits

6.1.2 Blockchain in Finance

Figure 6.1 signifies the tests and benefits of blockchain technology in various financial services, highlighting the main problems and advantages across various sectors, including e-finance, banking, insurance, digital payments, risk management, and fraud detection. Furthermore, blockchain technology has revolutionised frequent aspects of finance by enhancing transparency, privacy, and security, allowing fast settlements, modernising risk management, simplifying auditing, and reducing costs. These qualities convert traditional financial processes and organisations, creation them more efficient, secure, and accountable.

6.1.3 Emerging Trends in Blockchain Finance

Figure 6.2 illustrates the transformative impact of blockchain in finance in key areas such as transparency, privacy, security, fast settlements, risk management, auditing, and cost minimisation. These features demonstrate how blockchain technology is reshaping traditional financial processes and organisations. In addition to these progressions, blockchain has rapidly transformed various sectors, particularly finance, by presenting innovative frameworks like asset tokenisation and decentralised autonomous organisations (DAOs). This literature review synthesises recent research on these topics, emphasising their possibility to disturb and revolutionise traditional financial systems.

73

6.1.4 Tokenisation of Assets

Tokenisation is the process of changing physical or digital assets into blockchain-based tokens. This invention allows fractional ownership, recovers liquidity, and streamlines transactions. According to recent studies, tokenisation is an indispensable element in forming the World Innovation Stock Exchange, where the revolution of tokenisation and the securitisation of project management are grave (source). This suggests that tokenisation democratises entree to investment opportunities and raises better transparency and competence in asset management. Furthermore, the request for decentralised exchanges is energetic for the seamless conversation of these digital tokens and cryptocurrencies on the blockchains. The author highlighted that mixing decentralised exchanges within the decentralised finance (DeFi) ecosystems is energetic for the efficient trading of assets, thereby improving market dynamics and liquidity [12].

6.1.5 Decentralised Autonomous Organisations

DAOs signify another transformative trend in blockchain finance. These organisations operate on smart contracts and are ruled by their members, eradicating the traditional hierarchical structures. According to the researcher, DAOs have the potential to disrupt traditional funding mechanisms in various industries, particularly entertainment. Through the utilisation of blockchain tokens, DAOs can enable direct funding from stakeholders, thereby offering a more democratised method of investment and project management [13].

6.1.6 Security Challenges and Trust in Blockchain

Even though it has benefits, blockchain technology is not deprived of challenges. He recognises several security concerns, including the vulnerabilities to cyber threats, which could deteriorate the truthfulness of the financial transactions [14]. The joint 74of blockchain with outdated financial security instruments grants an area ready for further research, particularly in developing robust cybersecurity summaries custom-made to the blockchain environments.

6.1.7 Blockchain's Impact on Auditing and Corporate Governance

The inferences of blockchain technology spread into auditing and corporate governance. He argues that the blockchain can alter auditing through transparency and accountability in financial reporting [15]. This transformation stances questions about the future parts of the auditors and the potential need for new skill sets that contribute to blockchain knowledge. As organisations progressively accept blockchain for financial record-keeping, additional research is desirable to understand how these changes will mark the corporate governance structures and the compliance requirements.

6.2 Review of Literature

Blockchain has emerged as a transformative potency in numerous industries, with finance as the lead of its adoption. Recent studies have discovered the likelihood of blockchain in finance [15]. Blockchain is a transformative technology that can improve the speed, correctness, and cost-efficiency of financial transactions, possibly leading to extensive fluctuations in how firms function and devise new ways of payment through cryptocurrencies. The financial industry has already been activated to discover and implement blockchain-based solutions, along with applications that range from cross-border payments to trade finance and asset management [6].

In addition, blockchain technology’s decentralised and safe nature opens up new possibilities for financial inclusion, particularly where traditional banking services are rare [16]. It seeks to evaluate the possibility of DeFi replacing traditional finance by using the Ethereum platform enabled by blockchain. The abolition of the intermediaries and the mechanisation of the keen contracts result in cost reductions. Market share is gained by fintech companies working with blockchain startups. Limitations include industry-specific differences and long-term data availability. Implications call for more investigation into long-term effects, research particular to subsectors, and comparative evaluations. Fintech companies are urged to deliberately implement blockchain with a focus on risk management and compliance [5].

6.2.1 Transparency, Privacy, and Security

The decentralised ledger of blockchain guarantees transparency by authenticating the transactions through computers, which allows all participants to view them in real-time. Every transaction is tightly encrypted and cannot be improved in the past without the participants’ agreement. This transparency nurtures trust among the parties and diminishes the risk of deceit and employment. Blockchain technology is transformative in reshaping society and industry because of the fintech revolution and web utilisation [17]. According to this research, blockchain execution has been accepted to foster transparency and trust across various sectors due to increased 75competition in the digital landscape [18]. Integrating blockchain and artificial intelligence has changed business processes, increased efficiency and transparency and provided security to businesses [19]. Moreover, blockchain improved financial inclusion through various solutions, particularly in developing countries, and it can be made imaginable through IoT.

6.2.2 Fast Settlements

Blockchain tolerates fast settlements, avoiding the need for intermediaries and clearinghouses commonly created in old-fashioned financial systems. Smart contracts allow transactions to be automatically verified and settled founded on predefined conditions, as the agreement terms have been inscribed into the code. This automation reduces the time and cost related to the manual verification and processing.

6.2.3 Risk Management

Blockchain recovers risk management in finance, assuming that it has transparent and indisputable records of transactions. Financial institutions can use custom blockchain-based platforms to display and scrutinise transactions in real-time by more competently identifying the possible risks and anomalies.

6.2.4 Auditing

Auditing has become more efficient and dependable with blockchain technology. Auditors can authenticate the truthfulness of financial records without trusting third parties to settle the records.

6.2.5 Cost Minimisation

Blockchain weakens the costs in finance by eliminating intermediaries and eliminating manual processes. Smart contracts systematise the transaction clearances and implement the contract terms without the essential intermediaries such as banks or clearinghouses, thereby dipping the transaction fees and operational costs.

6.3 Research Methodology

The process begins with the expression of the key research questions designed to influence the primary advantages of blockchain technology in the respective financial sector, categorising the difficulties and constraints related to its implementation, measuring its influence on the various financial services, and discovering the emerging trends. Subsequently, a complete search strategy is developed using academic resources such as IEEE Xplore, Google, Science Direct, SpringerLink, and JSTOR. Keywords such as “Blockchain,” “Machine Learning,” “Finance Industry,” and “Regulatory” are working to answer the search. Specific inclusion criteria (IC) are recognised to select the works for presence in the review. These standards comprise keywords such as “Blockchain,” “fintech,” “distributed ledger technology,” and 76“Blockchain technology adoption” for IC 1. Rational operators are applied to define the standards’ composition.

Furthermore, the studies published before December 31, 2019, are omitted (IC 2), although only the research publications in English are measured (IC 3). The study types are restricted to journal articles (IC 4), and studies based on abstracts are included (IC 5). Furthermore, studies based on full texts are incorporated (IC 6). To eliminate literature from consideration for this systematic literature review, exclusion criteria (EC) are applied. Duplicate studies with identical titles and/or digital object identifiers are removed, and studies are eliminated based on quality ratings as specified in the exclusion conditions. At this stage, 42 studies were identified, of which 27 were deemed relevant to this investigation. The selected papers considered for this study are itemised in Table 6.1.

6.4 Results, Discussion, and Findings

Based on the above discussion and systematic literature review, it is apparent that most research employs both qualitative and quantitative analyses. The qualitative studies are analysed using the systematic literature review method. At the same time, the quantitative analyses use various statistical software and tools such as SPSS AMOS and methods such as descriptive and inferential analysis. Numerous important discoveries are highlighted in the comprehensive literature study on the influence of blockchain technology on the respective financial sector. Blockchain technology power facilitates increased efficiency and decreased expenses by removing the mediators and restructuringthe financial operations.

6.5 Implications of Blockchain in Finance

Blockchain technology can have a number of important repercussions for the financial sector. One of the most noteworthy aspects is the potential to revolutionise the payment systems. Blockchain technology permits individuals to conduct transactions directly with one another without the need for intermediaries. This results in a growth in transaction speed and a decrease in transaction costs. An additional benefit of this decentralised model is that it increases transparency and reduces the risk of fraud, which is an important concern in outdated financial systems.

Moreover, blockchain can justify the procedure of securities trading and settlement. By using keen contracts, the blockchain platforms allow the automatic execution of contracts once predefined conditions are met, eliminating the need for mediators such as clearing houses and dipping settlement times. This capability improves efficiency and drops the functioning risks and costs associated with the post-employment processes.

6.6 Conclusion

Blockchain technology has enhanced the financial sector by creating a secure and decentralised platform for various financial claims. There is an opportunity for the introduction of FinTech explanations based on blockchain technology to revolutionise 7778the distribution of financial services, which will result in improved accessibility, reduced expenses, and greater scrutiny. Various blockchain applications have emerged across numerous industries, including healthcare, the Internet of Things, security, and supply chain management. This is because blockchain has made it possible to construct a storage system that is decentralised, secure, and conspicuous. Blockchain technology has the potential to transform many different banking procedures, which means that it might significantly impact the financial sector. The power of blockchain technology has revolutionised the financial industry, giving rise to DeFi. This new method of financial services is shadowed by its decentralised countryside, innovative solutions, seamless interoperability, global reach, and supreme transparency. By approving DeFi, we can temporary financial inclusion, encourage open access, stimulate unrestricted novelty, and unlock the world of options for entrepreneurs and visionaries. From the industry perspective, blockchain technology significantly enhances efficiency by streamlining transactions, improving security through decentralisation, and fostering transparency with a tamper-proof ledger.
