15 Harnessing Blockchain for Biotechnology Current Applications, Challenges, and Future Opportunities

Asad Khan, Mohd. Aquib Ansari, Arvind Mewada, Greetta Pinheiro, and Amrendra Singh Yadav

DOI: 10.1201/9781003545620-19

15.1 Introduction

Blockchain [1, 2, 3], a decentralised and immutable ledger technology, has gained attention far beyond its initial application in cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin. By enabling secure, transparent, and tamper-resistant record-keeping, blockchain has the potential to transform various industries, including finance, supply chain management, and healthcare. The biotechnology sector has also begun exploring blockchain to solve some of its most pressing challenges in recent years. Biotechnology [4,5,6,7], a field that applies biological systems and organisms to develop products and technologies, is central to advancements in medicine, agriculture, and environmental sustainability.

Supply chains have indeed a very complicated structure, coupled with huge amounts of data generated and intellectual property (IP) protection in high demand. With biotechnology blossoming, managing and securing data, the integrity of research, and transparency along the supply chain also grow challenges. The inherent challenges push one into the adoption of blockchain technology, especially in biotechnology. As it is evident from the fact that biotechnology requires huge volumes of genomic data as well as clinical trial results or research findings, data management indeed becomes an overdue priority along with security matters. Figure 15.1 illustrates the blockchain’s overall architecture for data-sharing systems in bioinformatics. Traditional systems often fail to ensure such countermeasures against data breaches, unauthorised access, and manipulation of research data.

Blockchain technology indeed offers an impressive way out by providing such a decentralised, secure, and immutable record of transactions. In addition, the biotechnology industry encounters great challenges in IP management. The patenting processes of biotechnological innovations are often contested and complex, leading to litigation and disputes among the stakeholders. In this regard, blockchain can 184ease IP management by providing a transparent and immutable record of innovations, enabling the tracking and management of patents and licenses granted to the record owner.

Ultimately, the biotechnology retail chain, which comprises different agents including manufacturers, analysts, controllers, and, at last, retailers, has emerged as a prominent player. An important feature of these supply chains usually guarantees their security along with quality, hence remaining highly transparent and traceable throughout. In addition to preventing counterfeiting and adhering to regulatory requirements, the capacity of blockchain to provide a verifiable record of each step in the supply chain can contribute to the resolution of these issues. This review chapter aims to provide a far-reaching outline of the ongoing biotechnology applications for blockchain innovation.

In this chapter, Section 15.2 provides a synopsis of the principal thoughts behind blockchain innovation, including its most significant highlights and types. In section 3, 185the utilisation of blockchain in biotechnology, for example, information the board, protected innovation the executives, store network straightforwardness, and customised medication, are analysed. Section 15.4 discusses the troubles, impediments, and specialised, administrative, and reception hardships of carrying out blockchain in biotechnology. Section 15.5 comprehensively examines existing arrangements, including various blockchain stages and a review of contextual studies. Section 15.6 frames open doors and future exploration headings for blockchain and biotechnology combination. In the last section, the chapter comes to a close with a summary of the most significant findings and some concluding thoughts on the significance of blockchain in biotechnology in the future.

15.2 Blockchain Fundamentals

Most of the time, blockchain technology [8] is a distributed record framework that records transactions between various organisational computers. While traditional databases store data in a centralised location, blockchain operates on a decentralised network. All participants (nodes) have instant access to the same data as a result of this. This decentralisation is necessary for the transparency and security of the blockchain. The blockchain works by recording every transaction in a “block” linked to the previous block. Thus, a chain of blocks is formed, which is called a “blockchain.” Data in these blocks is secured by cryptographic algorithms, thereby ensuring that once a transaction is recorded, it is unchangeable. The consensus mechanisms vary depending on the design of the specific blockchain, which controls the addition of a new block to the chain. The consensus algorithm is the process of agreement by all participants in a blockchain network concerning the state of the distributed ledger. The most used consensus mechanism among these is Proof of Work (PoW). Nodes solve difficult algorithms for determining the rightful owner of that data. The first node that solves the problem is given the right to append a new block and is awarded with cryptocurrency. It, however, does involve a lot of energy consumption. Typically, the Proof of Stake (PoS) is considered more efficient than PoW, as a node’s probability of successfully adding a new block correlates with the number of tokens under its control. This work is said to consume minimal energy and is considered highly scalable.

Furthermore, Delegated Proof of Stakes enhances operation substantially since token holders get to nominate a certain cadre of delegates who will take responsibility for authenticating transactions and adding new blocks. Much quicker than PoW and PoS, the Delegated Proof of Stakes process has additional benefits. It applies mechanisms such as Byzantine Fault Tolerance to ensure that a blockchain can successfully operate, even with nodes resisted or erratic behaviour of nodes. This property is particularly important for private or consortium-like blockchains. In general, the features of cryptography, decentralised databases, transparency, and stability render blockchain technology superbly ideal for the industry’s areas where credit is valued and where data integrity and security are most important, being biotechnology. The fundamental principles of cryptography, decentralised databases, transparency, and structural foundation make blockchain especially appropriate for industries where the integrity of credit is paramount, together with data authenticity and security, such as biotechnology.

186

15.2.1 Blockchain Types and Platforms

Three main categories of blockchain technology are mostly classified as public, private, and consortium. Examples of public blockchains include Bitcoin and Ethereum. These blockchains are open to everyone and completely decentralised. These types of blockchains may serve a significant role in biotechnology because their characteristics are critical for the transparent verification of information, especially when it comes to data from clinical trials. However, private blockchains are restricted to only one entity or a collection of organisations. They are mostly found in industries like banking and those that rely on supply chains, where privacy and efficiency are issues. In biotechnology, these private blockchains can be used to store sensitive patient information or move proprietary research data securely. Consortium blockchains are halfway decentralised and managed by a group of institutions and not by a single institution. Thus, they greatly balance openness and privacy and are pertinent to addressing collaboration challenges in biotechnology, like multi-centre clinical trials and consortium-based research initiatives.

Blockchain platforms have emerged to cater to specific needs in the biotechnology sector. For instance, Ethereum is known for its smart contract capability and is used to build decentralised applications across multiple industries, including biotechnology. It thus has the agility to automate even complex processes such as IP management and clinical trial workflows. Hyperledger Fabric is a modular, permissioned blockchain platform developed by the Linux Foundation; its current adoption in enterprises is due to factors such as scalability, privacy features, and plug-and-play components. Hyperledger Fabric can facilitate secure data sharing and supply chain management in biotechnology. Corda, initially tailored for the financial sector, stands out as a permissioned blockchain platform that prioritises interoperability and privacy. It is particularly adept at handling scenarios where multiple organisations need to share data without exposing it to all participants. This unique architecture makes Corda an invaluable tool in the biotechnology field, especially when it comes to managing contracts, safeguarding intellectual properties, and ensuring regulatory compliance.

15.2.2 Key Characteristics Relevant to Biotechnology

Some unique properties of blockchain technology make it an essential application in biotechnology. Above all, it immutably means that once data in a blockchain have been entered, they cannot be altered in any way. This peculiarity is necessary for maintaining data integrity in the biotechnology preservation of clinical trials and research, as well as in IP/documentation. Another very important advantage is a high degree of transparency; implementation of a blockchain system makes it possible for all the stakeholders in an organisation to be able to access the same information, thus increasing transparency and diminishing possible errors or fraudulent conduct. This is highly relevant in both clinical trials and supply chain management contexts. A prominent feature of blockchain technology is its decentralised quality.

It wipes out vulnerability due to weak links and eliminates single-point control, all by eliminating central authority. This feature proves to be very beneficial in global 187supply chain and collaborative research environments. The other characteristic of blockchain technology is that it is highly secure since the cryptographic methods used by blockchain technology are resistant to data tampering as well as unauthorised access. Blockchain technology, in the field of biotechnology, where data protection is of utmost importance, serves as a viable approach to protecting sensitive data. Furthermore, self-executing agreements with terms directly encoded into programming code are termed smart contracts, which offer great advantages. Smart contracts minimise dependence on intermediaries, increase efficiency in operation, and enforce agreements without requiring third-party involvement. This can be useful in the biotechnology processes of licensing IP, management of clinical trials, and supply chain transactions.

15.3 Applications of Blockchain in Biotechnology

15.3.1 Supply Chain Management

This indicates that a supply chain for biotechnology benefits extensively from using blockchain in that it provides an open, timestamped record of transactions. Typical members of a biotechnological item manufacturing network include suppliers of unrefined substances, manufacturers, regulators, and distributors. Products must be traceable and authentic in the pharmaceutical industry because fake drugs will have dreadful implications. Modern studies have proved that blockchain technology can indeed increase the productive efficiency of production networks through its inalterable record of all supply chain transactions. One good example is the MediLedger project [9], which, by using blockchain, is tracing pharmaceutical drugs such that only genuine ones reach the end-users. Further research has been conducted using blockchain technology in agriculture, tracing and ensuring that the origin and integrity of Genetically Modified Organism (GMOs), among other biotechnology products, are verified.

The utilisation of VeChain [10] in the pharmaceutical industry is an outstanding application of blockchain technology in the biotechnology production network. VeChain’s blockchain platform enables pharmaceutical companies to track the entire lifecycle of drugs, from production to distribution. This prevents counterfeit goods from being distributed and ensures that regulatory standards are adhered to. The incorporation of blockchain with existing inventory network frameworks and the versatility of blockchain arrangements remain obstructions, even though blockchain offers critical benefits for inventory networks. Future assessments could explore hybrid models that unite blockchain with various advances, such as the Internet of Things, to further develop the creation of network-detectable quality and capability.

15.3.2 Data Management and Security

The biotechnology sector generates vast data, from genomic sequences [11] to clinical trial results. Managing and securing this data is a significant challenge, particularly given the sensitive nature of this information. Blockchain’s decentralised and secure architecture offers a promising solution for data management in biotechnology. 188Several studies have explored the use of blockchain for managing and securing biomedical data. For example, blockchain has been proposed to manage genomic data, where privacy and data ownership are critical concerns.

Projects such as the Personal Genome Project have experimented with using blockchain to give individuals control over their genomic data while ensuring it remains secure and private. Another project that is based on blockchain technology is the Iryo Network [12], which is an example of a platform that can implement the management of healthcare data. Through blockchain implementation, Iryo gives patients full control over their data—only individuals with appropriate rights can read the patient’s records. It can be generalised to manage genomic and other sensitive biotechnological information. However, as with most solutions, blockchain is not without problems and issues, including the problem of storage and issues of compliance. Further studies might identify how such solutions can be integrated into large biotechnological systems and how proper legal regulations supporting blockchain technology in managing big data can be implemented.

15.3.3 Intellectual Property and Licensing

A well-protected area of a biotechnological business is mainly based on an IP measure since the growth of genetics, pharmaceuticals, and other related ideas can only be protected through patents and licenses. IP administration and protection is not an easy thing since it requires the assistance of many parties, as well as compliance with several different legal systems. Applying the principles of blockchain to the realisation of IP in biotechnology can be an effective method of enhancing the security of the procedures and the easy record of ownership and other transactions in the field [11]. Some investigations revealed that blockchain technology is efficient and can be applied to IP rights such as patents, copyrights, and licenses. The idea of IP transactions captured on a blockchain will help reduce theft incidences and help track licenses and enforce them.

Other examples implemented to leverage blockchain include the Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS), which shows how blockchain could bring more efficiency to IP processes. The poet strategy [13] is an example of a blockchain-based solution for controlling computerised content freedoms. Even though Poet’s strategy was initially designed with digital media in mind, it could be applied to the management of IP in biotechnology to ensure that patents and licenses are transparently recorded and enforced. The intricacy of patent regulation, which changes fundamentally from one ward to another, is one of the principal hindrances to utilising blockchain for IP on the board. Blockchain, combined with existing patent and permitting frameworks and the production of normalised blockchain structures for IP boards, could be the subject of future exploration.

15.3.4 Clinical Trials and Research Integrity

Clinical preliminary studies are a fundamental component of biotechnology, particularly in developing novel drugs and treatments. However, concerns regarding the integrity of clinical trials are frequently sparked by issues such as manipulation of 189data, lack of transparency, and conflicts of interest. The unchanging and straightforward nature of blockchain makes it an ideal solution for ensuring the trustworthiness of examination and clinical preliminary information. The effectiveness of clinical trials has been the topic of several studies that have suggested using blockchain technology. For instance, Benchoufi and Ravaud [14] conclude that blockchain can timestamp and check each step of the clinical trial, which means that blockchain ensures data integrity and proper trial conduct. Another characteristic can also be traced back to the manipulation of trial results, and another key issue blockchain will assist pharmaceuticals with.

ClinTrial Token is an instance of how blockchain technology can be used to solve the problems of clinical trials. Since trial data is stored on a blockchain through ClinTrial Token, the data is reliable, transparent, and conform to the set standards. Overall, such an approach may go a long way in enhancing the reliability of trials, which in return enhances the investors’ certainty in the pharmaceutical business. Looking at the advantages of blockchain linked with clinical trial transparency, there are still issues, such as data privacy and the problem of its implementation across the industry. For future works, it could be possible to propose studies linking further transparency and privacy that could be implemented with blockchain and studies that could better incentivise blockchain usage in clinical trials.

15.3.5 Personalised Medicine and Genomics

One rapidly developing field of biotechnology is personalised medicine, which focuses on targeted therapies considering a patient’s genetic makeup. However, there are significant challenges related to the secure management and sharing of genetic data. Blockchain technology offers a promising solution specifically designed to protect sensitive information and facilitate the secure sharing of large data sets, such as genomic data. Multiple initiatives have been implemented in the application of blockchain in the field of Ph 4400. For instance, EncrypGen [15] uses blockchain to enable human beings to contribute markers of their genetics with researchers safely and of their own volition. Likewise, Nebula Genomics utilises blockchain to share genomics data, which people can sell to researchers or pharma companies.

The Shivom project is the blockchain technology system for genomic data sharing. Through blockchain, Shivom enables customers to share genomic data with researchers and pharmaceutical companies and simultaneously decide who should be able to use the information. What makes this approach beneficial is the possibility of propelling the research in personalised medicine without violating the individual’s rights to privacy. However, one of the major issues that need to be addressed when applying blockchain in the context of personal medicine is data protection on the one hand and the ability to share data for research purposes on the other. Further study can be done in the direction of adopting blockchain with privacy techniques so that the data can be shared securely without compromising the privacy of the individuals. However, it is also known that the applicability of blockchain solutions for handling massive genomic data is one of the essential concerns for the future.

190

15.4 Challenges and Limitations

15.4.1 Technical Challenges

Identifying the benefits that blockchain brings to the field of biotechnology is crucial. Researchers also encounter numerous technical issues in using blockchain technology, which include issues on scalability, interoperability, and energy use. As of now, scalability remains the most prominent technical problem in blockchain. Even public blockchains such as Bitcoin and Ethereum can only process a number of transactions in a certain amount of time, leading to wait times and high fees per transaction. This limitation is most pronounced for practical applications in biotechnology that need huge amounts of computation or involve thousands of transactions. Another major problem with blockchain technology is interoperability.

Data sharing and collaboration, which are imperative concepts in the field of biotechnology, suffer due to the inability of different blockchain systems to cooperate. For instance, data transfer between different types of blockchains is usually not possible, and hence, the application of blockchain technology is complex. Finally, energy consumption is one of the significant challenges as it severely hampers the functioning of PoW-based blockchain networks. The heavy energy requirement for the functioning of PoW-based blockchain networks has raised concerns about the environmental impact and sustainability of such systems over time. This is particularly relevant for industries like biotechnology, which is increasingly looking towards sustainable approaches.

15.4.2 Regulatory and Ethical Issues

Although there is a trend of prohibiting certain uses of blockchain, particularly for biotechnology-related applications, it is still tightly regulated, and various issues will have to be settled before they can be utilised. It matters that legal uncertainty threatens the whole application area, especially regarding the situation with blockchain-based transactions or smart contracts applied by it. It may particularly act as a deterrent in highly regulated industries such as biotechnology, where the stakes are really high. Data privacy is another major challenge, especially when it comes to the use of big data analytics.

The immutability of blockchain records raises ownership concerns over data. Again, in biotechnology, where sensitive data, especially genomic data, are collected, compliance with data privacy laws such as the General Data Protection Regulation becomes very important. Moreover, there are also ethical issues at this point in using blockchain technology in biotechnology. For instance, issues of data ownership and consent come into play. For example, personalised medicine raises questions about data ownership and the potential exploitation of genomic information for economic purposes, where sensitive data commercialisation goes beyond its ethical limits. These are ethical concerns that must be addressed to ensure that this technology is responsibly utilised within biotechnology.

191

15.4.3 Adoption and Implementation Challenges

Many issues have to be dealt with and bridged to catalyse the adoption of blockchain technology in the biotechnology industry and its application. Resistance to change will be the biggest challenge that the adoption of blockchain technology will face. Most of the stakeholders here have spent decades within organisations relying much on conventional technologies, making it hard for them to shift to blockchain systems. High expense or sometimes even exorbitantly extravagant cost is a considerable barrier. The cost of implementing and maintaining the solutions using blockchain is really extremely high.

The financial advantages might accrue from its use over time, but in the end, investment in development and integration would be extremely limited due to its short-term understanding. Complexity does not facilitate adoption into blockchain as well. The chains in technology are complex, while the skills required in developing blockchain solutions are very specialised. This can be a big barrier for organisations without the relevant human resource profile because they cannot adopt and effectively use the technology.

15.5 Comparative Analysis of Existing Solutions

Based on the potential uses and varying characteristics of the blockchain in the biotechnology sector, various blockchain platforms are available. In this section, the authors describe the most promising blockchain solutions to be applied in biotechnology and compare them with advantages and disadvantages for specific tasks.

Ethereum vs. Hyperledger Fabric: Ethereum is very flexible and allows the support of smart contracts, making it suitable for use in IP management and clinical trial processes. It is a public platform, however, with scalability issues that make it less appropriate for dealing with sensitive data. On the other hand, Hyperledger Fabric is an open-source Blockchain Consortium (BCC) that is privacy-enhancing and flexible to use while implementing smart contracts; this suits large-scale organisations that use it in a supply chain and secure information exchange.

Corda vs Quorum: Corda is permissioned and also open, and therefore, it is well suited for establishing platforms through which different organisations can safely share data. Like Quorum, which is based on Ethereum but has granted access only to certain participants, the provision of anonymity in Vital is combined with the possibility of using a smart contract. It would be highly appropriate for both platforms to handle the various contracts and comply with biotechnology regulations; however, the colour choice will depend on the needs of each application.

This section also discusses several real-world cases of the successful application of blockchain in biotechnology, as well as an assessment of the effectiveness of such approaches and their potential consequences.

MediLedger Project: One of the projects that prove blockchain improves the supply chain and prevents the distribution of counterfeit products is MediLedger, which employs blockchain in tracking pharmaceutical products. This, therefore, 192shows how the use of blockchain enhances the safety and compliance with the standards of biotechnological products.

EncrypGen: Blockchain-based applications such as EncrypGen, which is used to manage genomic data through the blockchain, have described how blockchain can help people control how their data and information are used and shared securely. These sentiments apprise the platform’s effectiveness and the potential facilitated by blockchain to overhaul data in personalised medication.

IPOS Blockchain Patent Platform: The IPOS has implemented blockchain technology to manage patents. The danger of patent disputes has been eliminated, and the patenting process has been accelerated, proving the viability of the application of blockchain platforms for managing all forms of IP in biotechnology.

15.6 Future Directions and Research Opportunities

Integrating blockchain technology with other relatively modern technologies, artificial intelligence [16,17,18,19,20], the Internet of Things, and big data presents great opportunities for developing biotechnology. For instance, integrating blockchain with artificial intelligence can make treatment planning and patient data analysis more effective in personalised medicine. Likewise, integrating blockchain with the Internet of Things may improve accountability in the supply chain for biotechnological products by allowing for tracking services. Although progress has been made in applying blockchain technology to biotechnology, there are still a number of research obstacles. These include developing standard structures for blockchain reception in biotechnology, working on the adaptability and interoperability of blockchain arrangements, and developing protection-saving blockchain advancements. Blockchain could affect biotechnology by making it conceivable to oversee information in a safer and viable way, expanding the straightforwardness of supply chains and shielding protected innovation. Notwithstanding, using this potential will require progressing blockchain innovation examination, joint effort, and speculation.

15.7 Conclusion

Blockchain technology can address some of the most pressing issues in biotechnology, such as supply chain transparency, IP management, and data security. In any case, a couple of particular regulatory and gathering difficulties should be addressed to grasp this potential. The primary focus of subsequent research should be overcoming these obstacles and examining the emerging opportunities at the intersection of blockchain and biotechnology.

16 Blockchain and Artificial Intelligence in Financial Industry 4.0 Enter the World of Digital Transformation

Annu and Ravindra Tripathi

DOI: 10.1201/9781003545620-21

16.1 Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the ability of a computer or machine to mimic human intelligence and conduct. Trend analysis, stock price predictions, fraud detection, and routine work automation are all possible with AI in finance. In recent years, significant advances have been made in AI technology. Google Inc.’s Alpha-Go AI software defeated human Go players in 2016, placing machine learning at the top of the rankings. After that, machine learning, neural networks, and other terms became common in financial markets and stock exchanges. Technology like AI and finance Industry 4.0 are changing the financial services business. Programming computers to learn, make judgments, and recognise patterns from past lessons is called “artificial intelligence” (AI). However, financial Industry 4.0 refers to adopting modern technologies like AI, big data, and blockchain in financial services [1,2].

Blockchain technology has transformed financial transactions by enhancing security and speed [3]. Asset tokenisation, cross-border payments, and smart contracts are further blockchain finance applications. The transaction will determine the ideal blockchain for finance. Private blockchains are better for private transactions, while public blockchains are transparent. Transaction speed, security, and regulatory compliance are critical when choosing financial blockchain models. Financial activity type also affects this choice. Blockchain records transactions transparently and unchangeably, improving financial operations. Due to its decentralised nature, fraud and manipulation are considerably reduced [4,5]. Fintech companies use AI and its many applications to create digital trading platforms that allow low-income women and young and small businesses to access the mainstream financial market.

AI and blockchain in the finance Industry 4.0 are solving risk management, fraud detection, and portfolio optimisation problems. AI also helps financial institutions offer real-time financial data and 24/7 client service. AI and blockchain in the financial Industry 4.0 are launching a new age of innovation and growth in financial services that might improve efficiency, accuracy, and accessibility for businesses and customers.

198

16.1.1 Industries Revolution Background

  • Coal in 1765: Steam power and manufacturing mechanisation began in the 18th century, starting the First Industrial Revolution. Mechanised spinning wheels produced eight times as much thread as conventional ones in the same period. Steam was noted for its efficacy. Its industrial use was the most significant productivity boost. Without humans, steam engines could power weaving looms. Technology like the steamship and (100 years later) the steam-powered locomotive allowed people and goods to travel farther in less time, leading to further advances.
  • Gas in 1870: With the rise of electricity and the production line in the 19th century, the Second Industrial Revolution began. Henry Ford (1863–1947) invented mass manufacturing in a Chicago abattoir where pigs were hung from conveyor belts, and each butcher only slaughtered a piece. “Henry Ford (1863–1947) implemented these concepts into automotive manufacturing, transforming the industry.” Previously, an entire car was assembled at one location; now, small batches on a conveyor belt are more efficient and cost-effective.
  • Electronics and Nuclear in 1969: The decade of the 1970s marked the beginning of the 20th century’s Third Industrial Revolution with the use of computers and memory-programmable controls. Since these technologies were introduced, production can be automated without human interaction. Well-known examples are robots that run pre-programmed sequences without human interaction.

  • Internet and Renewable Energy in 2000: “Industry 4.0” refers to corporate use of information and communication technology, building on advancements from the Third Industrial Revolution. Using a network link, “an online digital twin can be established and expanded for computer-based manufacturing processes.” These allow facilities to communicate with one another and transmit information about themselves [6, 3]. Smart factories are created by cyber-physical production systems that connect all systems and require minimal human interaction. When these enablers come together, Industry 4.0 could revolutionise manufacturing. Examples are machines that foresee problems and start repair operations or self-organised logistics that adjust to production variations. Figure 16.1 depicts the Industrial Revolution.

199

16.1.2 Involvement of Technologies

Figure 16.2 shows technological advances like cashless payments, digital payments, and Internet banking affect everyone daily. Investment technology is evolving, as shown by online trading apps. AI and machine learning improve digital market administration.

The stock market is complex and dynamic. Selecting an effective investment plan is tough. The challenge is accurate prediction. Stock prices are affected by politics, the market, and the economy. Investor decisions also affect them. Circumstances can significantly affect stock prices. Strict analysis makes finding a simple linear function equation for stock prices and other parameters difficult. Thus, while many basic investing models can recommend investments, they rarely foresee irregular financial goods. AI involves self-organisation, nonlinearity, learning, and self-adaptation.

16.2 Theoretical Framework and Conceptual Model

16.2.1 Artificial Intelligence and Stock Trading Industry 4.0 Relation

Modern financial markets can simplify market operations and increase trading strategy versatility. Financial institutions now operate better thanks to AI and machine learning [7]. From opening an online demat account to trading, everything is electronic. Technology improves usefulness and does not replace intelligence [8]. Financial markets today rely on trading software and transaction analysis instruments. Many trading systems allow online trading and demat accounts.

200Stock Trading Industry 4.0 uses cutting-edge technology like AI to improve stock trading efficiency and efficacy. AI’s purpose in Stock Trading Industry 4.0 is to analyse enormous amounts of data in real-time and make predictions and judgments. Additional trading solutions that employ AI to improve your trading experience are available. See how technology generates investor intelligence:

  • Risk Awareness: Businesses leverage machine learning, processing speed, and big data to analyse compliance risk-taking. This results from AI technology helping investors recognise complex trading patterns on a large scale. It also occurs in real-time across all marketplaces.
  • AI Stock Trading: Real-time financial notes, data, trending firms, and market information enable investors to trade. This is done via speech recognition and Natural Language Processing (NLP). Its primary benefit is saving traders time and effort.
  • Recommendations and Tips: Stock recommendations are made available through recognition technology, which helps investors make smart choices and maximise certain trading opportunities.
  • Less Human Error: because traders do not have to interact with people to get advice on trading tactics, etc. Data science quickly overcomes investment challenges.

16.2.1.1 Major Steps for the Formation of AI in the Financial Industry

Various steps, including AI in the financial industry, can be considered, as shown in Figure 16.3.

  • Data Collection and Preparation: The first step is to gather and process vast amounts of financial data to feed into AI algorithms.
  • Model Development: This involves selecting appropriate AI algorithms and developing models that can analyse financial data and make predictions or recommendations.
  • Training and Validation: The models have to be trained in big data so that accuracy improves; after that, these are validated to ensure effectiveness.
  • Integration and Deployment: AI models must be integrated with existing financial systems and deployed to end-users.
  • 201Monitoring and Maintenance: After their development, the AI models are monitored for performance and updated accordingly to ensure effectiveness.
  • Regulation and Ethical Considerations: The financial services industry is highly regulated. It should, therefore, develop and deploy AI in full consideration of the existing laws and regulations while exercising concern for ethical considerations.

16.2.2 Major Area of Financial Technology in Industry 4.0

FinTech represents one of the economy’s fastest-growing sectors, using technology to improve and automate financial services. Major FinTech applications in Industry 4.0 include:

  • Mobile and Digital Banking: Greater penetration of mobiles and internet connectivity has also transformed the level of mobile banking and mobile merchant services.
  • Blockchain Technology: Blockchain technology increases financial transaction transparency, security, and efficiency.
  • Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning: AI and machine learning will automate most finance processes regarding risk management, fraud detection, and the management of investments.
  • Robo-Advisors: Automated investment management services, often called robo-advisors, are becoming increasingly popular because they offer personalised investment advice to individuals.
  • Digital Currencies: Digital currencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum are becoming more mainstream, leading to a growing interest in expanding new financial products and services based on blockchain technology.
  • Insurtech: FinTech companies are transforming the insurance sector by offering new products, services, and distribution channels, leveraging digital and data technologies.

16.2.2.1 How Has AI Made Its Mark in Financial Industry 4.0?

The financial industry’s theoretical framework for AI is based on several key concepts and principles. One key concept is using machine learning algorithms that analyse and process large amounts of financial data, such as market trends, customer behaviour, and risk factors. Another important concept is using artificial neural networks to make predictions and decisions based on this data.

As seen in Figure 16.4, the conceptual model of AI in the financial sector usually consists of the following elements:

  • Data Processing and Analysis: The AI algorithms extract, clean, and process financial data for further use.
  • Machine Learning Algorithms: These algorithms use algorithms that have potential, such as decision trees, random forests, and neural networks, to analyse and make predictions on processed financial data.
  • 202Predictive Modelling: This employed the output from machine learning algorithms to procure prognostications about the future trends in the marketplace, customers’ behaviour, and risk factors.
  • Decision-Making: This implies the application of the predictive modelling module in decision-making processes, such as finding the best approach to investments or minimising risks.
  • Overall, the conceptual model of AI in the financial industry aims to use advanced technologies and algorithms to improve decision-making and enhance the efficiency of financial operations.

16.2.2.2 How Has Blockchain Technology Made Its Mark in Financial Industry 4.0?

Blockchain is essential and promising in Industry 4.0 [9,10], and this technology is believed to transform the world economy. It offers many chances for established businesses to prosper and new ones to start while challenging traditional enterprises. Blockchain is mainly connected with Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies. Its benefits extend beyond cryptocurrency to many commercial and social transactions. 203Thus, blockchain could be used in different business applications [11,12]. Blockchain’s strong cryptographic encryption, network participants’ ongoing monitoring, and decentralised transaction data make it fraud-resistant. These features make manipulating system transactions nearly impossible [13,14].

Figure 16.5 illustrates how blockchain technology affects numerous facets of the financial industry by offering decentralised, transparent, safe, and efficient solutions.

16.3 Theoretical and Practical Implications

16.3.1 Why Should I Feel Confident Investing in Artificial Intelligence?

Face recognition on phones, online shopping recommendations, finding the perfect job, a tailored music list, and Google Maps to handle intricate and unpredictable traffic are all examples of AI making our lives easier. AI affects us unknowingly [15]. AI-powered ‘Jarvis Invest creates and manages a portfolio using 12 million financial criteria. We manage risk with this portfolio’s 24 × 7 risk management. It can eliminate standard financial measuring methods’ flaws in complex settings [16]. Indeed, quantitative investment using machine learning and AI has advanced swiftly and benefited investors.

204

16.3.2 Applications and Challenges of AI in Stock Market Industry 4.0

AI is employed in the stock trading sector in various applications, as illustrated in Figure 16.6.

  • Portfolio Management: Using parameters like risk tolerance, investment horizon, and performance objectives, AI algorithms can be utilised to optimise the composition of a portfolio of investments.
  • Development of Trading Strategies: AI may be used to find relationships and patterns in massive data sets that can be utilised to create trading strategies. These tactics may be based on fundamental analysis, technical analysis, or a mix of the two.
  • Trade Execution: AI can automatically execute trades based on preset parameters or rules. Circumstances set in algorithms tracking markets and then executing trades when such circumstances are filled can be used.
  • 205Risk Management: With real-time monitoring of trades and portfolios, AI analyses and controls risks once they occur. Examples include detecting unusual trading patterns, noticing market conditions, and making any necessary changes in the trades based on them [5].
  • Market Analysis: With market data analysis, AI can provide insight for traders making the right decisions, like finding patterns and trends from market data, predicting price changes, or even giving real-time market analyses.

AI may increase equity trading efficiency, reduce cost, and enhance accuracy. However, AI is only the most accurate if its data and algorithms are the best; errors or biases in these will lead to errors [17]. In actively managed equity funds, AI advisers replace advisers when picking stocks. BlackRock is the most prominent US investment manager stock picker with a self-learning AI-based investment program. AI stock trading employs Robo-Advisors that scan for vast data and make a trade at optimal timing and price. AI traders are more visionary and effectively control a company’s corporate trades, reducing risks and earning more returns [18,19]. Still, the financial sector faces many challenges in embracing AI technology. One of the main setbacks is the absence of technical people trained and skilled enough to set up AI systems.

The cost of AI is expensive in terms of purchase and large-scale implementation. Privacy issues also arise due to the immense amounts of data AI systems need to function effectively, posing security issues to financial institutions. More automation via AI also leads to job loss and, hence, the redeployment of workers. It is limited to the accuracy because also by the quality of data on which the AI systems have been trained that sometimes will convey biases in the resultant output. Many consumers still doubt AI in the financial sector, as they always distrusted an AI-powered system where they will keep storing their finances and other assets [20]. The deployment of an AI system is technically cumbersome as it has to interface with the existing processes. There is also a talent shortage in AI, making it difficult for financial institutions to find qualified professionals to develop and implement these systems. Lastly, the high costs associated with AI development and implementation can make it challenging for institutions to justify the investment.

Among the challenges that emerge from AI in finance are lack of transparency or bias by a financial AI system, data quality, regulation, expertise, risk management, and black box algorithms. Financial AI algorithms are complex, and an investor finds it challenging to evaluate AI-based investment strategies. Biassed AI systems could lead to the wrong financial output. AI algorithms generate forecasts based on the large amounts of data available and quality counts for precision [6]. It is challenging for investors to analyse AI-powered investment risks because they are not precisely controlled and regulated in finance. The topic of AI is expanding very fast, and many investors cannot appreciate the risks and benefits associated with AI-powered investment techniques. AI algorithms can process large amounts of data quickly, offering real-time financial choices that complicate risk management for investors. AI algorithms can indeed be “black box” systems, making investment decisions incomprehensible or impossible for investors to understand. The above issues thus underpin 206the importance of an informed investor being well-informed about the potential dangers and benefits of AI-powered investment strategies and the deliberative nature of the investment.

16.4 Conclusion, Implications, and Future Research Directions

As a contribution to the finance literature, the paper further exposes an analysis of the role of AI within the financial industry as launched by the Fourth Industrial Revolution, Industry 4.0. It portrays the technological evolution from the first industrial revolution and draws insights into AI and stock trading as part of financial technology, or FinTech 4.0. The research shows how AI and blockchain change the financial sector by providing better safety, efficiency, and inclusivity at lower costs and without intermediaries. Given this pattern, technology can further impact the financial sector and provide growth opportunities.

Industry 5.0 would be the shift from technology-centric processes to human–machine collaboration. As such, Industry 5.0 would emphasise the integration of AI with human expertise, in turn, being able to produce highly personal, efficient, and innovative outputs (see Figure 16.7). Therefore, if manufacturing and financial services fail to keep pace with changes in the sector, Industry 5.0 will make them obsolete.

207While AI brings sundry advantages, high cost remains one of the main barriers. The costs of implementing AI on efficiency and privacy must be overcome so financial institutions can fully adopt and implement AI. Future directions should be to make technologies more accessible and affordable.

Moreover, future research should conduct surveys on investors to assess their knowledge about AI and how complete AI integration can impact investment choices. Further research into AI synergy with new technologies may lead to better decisions that benefit investors and businesses. AI can be fully utilised in the financial sector by addressing concerns over cost and privacy.

17 International Payments Using Blockchain A Comprehensive Analysis of Efficiency, Security, and Feasibility

Arvind Mewada, Mohd. Aquib Ansari, Niharika Keshari, Nagendra Singh, and Amrendra Singh Yadav

DOI: 10.1201/9781003545620-22

17.1 Introduction

With the rapid development of internet technology, electronic money transfers or international payments are growing rapidly. Nowadays, the international payment system plays an important role in performing global e-commerce activities. The total value of global international payments has reached USD 11.53 trillion in 2024 and is estimated to increase to USD 21.8 trillion by 2028, as per the World Bank statistics [1]. India is a major global trading nation that generates a large volume of international payments due to its broad offline import and export activities. In addition, the demand for international payments in India is increasing day by day due to factors such as e-commerce transactions, studying abroad, and tourism.

Nonetheless, the existing international payment model is suffering from challenges such as cumbersome processes and high transaction fees. Moreover, as these payment systems are exposed to serious security threats, these can expose user privacy as well as data protection risks [2]. Even this system has lengthy processing times and inefficient capital usage, which have further hampered the growth of e-commerce. Therefore, addressing these challenges and optimising international payment methods have become an important research area in the international payment system.

The cryptocurrency Bitcoin introduces the groundbreaking concept of blockchain technology. This technology has transformed financial applications, particularly in digital payment systems, both nationally and internationally. The greatest advantage of blockchain is that it has the ability to secure transactions and foster trust at a lower cost. This kind of feature of blockchain has garnered significant attention from government institutions, organisations, technology-based companies, and financial institutions worldwide [3]. This is known as the first generation of blockchain technology.

210The second generation of blockchain technology introduced smart contracts, enabling functionalities beyond digital transaction transactions to assets such as stocks, loans, and real estate. The third generation of blockchain technology further expands its scope and offers solutions for industries ahead of banking and finance, such as healthcare, government, and even the science sector [4,5].

The National Institution for Transforming India (NITI Aayog) is a policy think tank for the government of India. NITI Aayog published a draft discussion paper in January 2020 titled “Blockchain: The India Strategy.” In this report, the Aayog highlighted the journey or development of blockchain technology within the country (India) [6]. The Indian government has initiated various blockchain initiatives across sectors to promote the technology and related industries. For instance, in February 2020, the “Maharashtra Blockchain Sandbox” was launched, focusing on blockchain-based applications for e-governance, particularly in supply chain management, land registry, and public record-keeping [7]. The IndiaChain project, established in 2017, also aimed to create a blockchain-based platform for exchanging information and services among government agencies [8].

In the banking sector, ICICI Bank of India integrated blockchain technology into its Internet e-commerce financing system in August 2016. Furthermore, in December 2022, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) launched the Digital Rupee, a central bank digital currency utilising blockchain technology. Unlike other cryptocurrencies, the Electronic Rupee (ER) has intrinsic value and is regulated by the RBI. The State Bank of India (SBI) Bank of Communications is also actively developing blockchain-based international payment application systems [9].

17.2 Related Work

Blockchain is a digital distributed ledger that employs cryptographic techniques to secure and link digital records known as “blocks.” These blocks are interconnected in sequential order through cryptographic “hashes,” which form a secure chain of blocks. The foundation principle of blockchain has evolved since the 1980s but has been popularised worldwide after the advent of Bitcoin. Chaum [10] performed an early innovation in which he proposed blind signatures. It is a cryptographic method that is used for automated payments while ensuring the payee, transaction amount, and timing remain anonymous to third parties. Performing advancements in the area of cryptography, Haber and Stornetta [11] presented the concept of timestamping digital documents. It enhances security and authenticity by using timestamps embedded in records.

The author Finney [12] performed further extended advanced research in this field with the Reusable Proof of Work concept. This represents a groundwork for a secure and transparent digital currency payment system that could operate independently of traditional banks or central authorities. This research contribution shows a conclusion in the form of the first Bitcoin transaction performed in 2009. In this transaction, the researcher transferred ten Bitcoin (BTC) to a friend, and this marks the appearance of blockchain technology.

Bhaskar and Chuen [13] established the first Bitcoin exchange named “Bitcoin Market.” It is marked a significant milestone for the blockchain development. 211Buterin [14] follows this and introduces the concept known as a smart contract, which is integral to Ethereum based on a blockchain platform designed for decentralised applications and transactions beyond digital currencies.

Swan [15] performed a study based on the application scope of blockchain technology. This study highlighted the potential of blockchain in the financial sector. Further ahead, Patki and Sople [16] analysed the impact of blockchain on traditional financial institutions. They find the influence of blockchain on Indian commercial banks. Zhang [17] explored the application of blockchain in international payments systems. The author notices the potential of blockchain to create a globally integrated clearing system and to reduce transaction costs.

Deng [18] analysed the innovative potential of blockchain in international payment systems. He suggested strategies for blockchain trial and broader promotion. Similarly, Mori [19] performed a case study on Ripple. He demonstrated the advantages of blockchain in payment and settlement processes. Li [20] examined the limitations of existing traditional international payment models. He provides details on the benefits of blockchain-based payment systems and highlights their challenges.

Shen et al. [21] proposed an international payment system based on blockchain. They describe the advantages of blockchain in simplifying transactions. Roy et al. [22] compared various blockchain payment models used in international payments. Deng [23] also highlighted the potential of blockchain to address the bottlenecks in traditional international payment systems. Despite these advantages, Deng warned that risks associated with the implementation of blockchain technology based on international payments still need thorough exploration.

The literature of this chapter reveals that inefficiency, high costs, and security risks are the most prominent challenges associated with traditional international payments. This makes these issues a focus point for researchers in this field of research. The advent of blockchain offers promising solutions to these pain points using the introduction of decentralised, tamper-proof, anonymous, and traceable systems.

This chapter explores the potential of blockchain technology to overcome the limitations of existing international payment systems. Initially, the chapter theoretically examines the advantages of blockchain, which simplifies the payment process, enhances payment efficiency, reduces transaction costs, and ensures the security and authenticity of transactions. Then, designed a case study of an international payment system based on blockchain, which integrates real-world operations. Finally, the chapter presents recommendations for implementing blockchain in international payments, offering valuable insights for developing and commercialising blockchain-based payment systems in India.

17.3 Blockchain Technology Overview

Blockchain synthesises distributed data storage, peer-to-peer (P2P) transmission, cryptographic algorithms, consensus mechanisms, timestamps, incentive structures (including rewards and punishments), and smart contracts. At its core, it is a decentralised, collectively maintained, and reliable ledger technology. Due to its decentralised, tamper-proof, anonymous, programmable, and secure nature, blockchain holds significant application value in areas such as digital currencies, international 212payments, and trade finance. Blockchain is composed of multiple blocks linked together to form a chain. Each block is structured with two main components, as depicted in Figure 17.1, representing a typical block structure: the block header and the block body.

The block body stores verified transactions, while the block header contains important metadata. This metadata includes the hash of the previous block, the hash of the current block, the timestamp, the nonce, and the Merkle root, all of which ensure the block’s integrity and its connection to the rest of the chain.

The blockchain architecture is divided into six layers, as shown in Figure 17.2. Among them, the data layer is used to describe the physical form of the blockchain. It primarily includes data blocks, hash functions, timestamps, Merkle trees, chain structure, public-key encryption, etc. In the network layer, there are distributed networking, communication, and data verification mechanisms to distribute, forward, and verify blockchain transactions, etc. Typically modelled as a P2P network for all nodes that are equal participants. As soon as a transaction occurs, it is sent to nearby nodes, which check whether it is valid or invalid according to the rules set. Valid transactions are forwarded to further nodes, and invalid ones are discarded. In digital signatures, asymmetric cryptography is used to authenticate transactions through a signing and verification phase. It ensures secure interactions and communication among nodes in the blockchain network. The consensus layer contains various algorithms that are designed to achieve efficient agreement among untrustworthy nodes in decentralised environments. Blockchain networks do not have a trusted central node, so a rule (protocol) or process is needed to obtain consensus before a block is added to the blockchain network. So, in this layer, four major (Proof of Work (PoW), Proof of Stake, Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (PBFT), and Delegated 213214Proof of Stake (DPoS)) consensus mechanisms are widely used. The PoW is utilised in Bitcoin, which requires nodes to repeatedly run hashing functions to generate a nonce that is difficult to produce yet easy to validate. The PoS is an energy-efficient mechanism that enables nodes with the largest stakes to generate blocks.

The DPoS is a type of blockchain consensus mechanism in which token holders elect delegates who create new blocks and verify transactions on the blockchain. This system is designed to make blockchain operations more democratic and efficient. PBFT is a consensus algorithm designed to reach consistent decisions in blockchains and distributed networks even when some nodes behave erratically or maliciously. It is specifically designed to solve the Byzantine Fault Tolerance problem of keeping the system secure and stable despite fraud or malfunctions in the network. The incentive layer contains issuance and distribution mechanisms, which are mainly used to encourage nodes to participate in the security verification of blockchain transactions. The contract layer contains various algorithms, such as script codes and smart contracts. These are used to realise programmable features. The application layer includes application scenarios and cases of blockchain in various fields.

The processes of recording, transmitting, verifying, and storing blockchain data do not require the credit endorsement of a third-party institution. Instead, they rely solely on mathematical methods that enable distributed nodes to achieve a consensus of trust. Blockchain systems employ P2P networks without a central server. This network structure comprises many highly autonomous nodes that are equal in status and freely connected in a flat topology, allowing for resource sharing. In blockchain, decentralisation reduces transaction complexity, saves costs, and alleviates issues (connection interruptions and information delays), which ensures efficient value transfer without intermediary (organisation or middleman) links or servers.

Blockchain is a key technology that uses cryptographic methods to ensure the security and tamper-freeness of data. Hash functions serve as a unique tool under this security layer, which plays a vital role in maintaining the authenticity and integrity of data. This hash function works as a strong collision resistance, which is used to link blocks. It ensures that transaction information remains intact. An individual node attempts to tamper with transaction data already uploaded to the blockchain. So, when this happens, the hash value changes, which makes the block with that transaction invalid. Other nodes reject any attempts to tamper with the data unless someone manages to control 51% of the entire network, which would make it possible to manipulate the blockchain. Otherwise, tampering with a single node has no effect due to the integrity of the blockchain. Strong computational protection against attacks is provided to the authorisation and the verification of transactions in the blockchain through a mechanism such as PoW based on public key cryptography.

Moreover, timestamp technology is used to add a time dimension to data, which ensures the traceability and authenticity of each transaction record. Smart contracts work as digital commitments that make blockchain data programmable, which is used to enhance the management and trading of traditional financial assets and lay the foundation for programmable financial systems. They are characterised by decentralisation and autonomy. Decentralisation means that smart contracts are executed by decentralised stored and verified program codes, ensuring fairness and equity in fund transfers. Autonomy implies that once specific conditions are met, the contract executes automatically without external interference, ensuring the security 215and accuracy of transaction processing. By leveraging the programmability of blockchain smart contracts, complex centralised clearing processes can be eliminated, significantly reducing costs, improving efficiency, and enabling the quick and convenient trading of financial products.

Although transaction information in the blockchain is broadcast to the entire network, the identities of the transaction nodes remain anonymous. Each node does not need to trust one another, meaning identity information must not be publicly disclosed. This allows for anonymity, protecting user privacy. Each account identity in the blockchain system is represented by a wallet address that can be changed at will. This wallet address is generated through cryptographic technology, making it impossible to infer the user’s identity or private key. No one can determine the identity of the transaction user corresponding to an account, ensuring that each transaction is carried out anonymously.

Blockchain is a distributed shared ledger maintained collectively by all nodes. The distributed data storage and transaction recording enable all users to participate in this bookkeeping system. The data on the ledger is public and transparent, allowing anyone to check, trace, and audit information through a public interface. This public transparency ensures the tamper-proof nature of blockchain data and allows for public oversight of compliance with operational behaviour. Consequently, the transaction information within the blockchain system is open and transparent, preventing one node from deceiving another. The transparency of blockchain promotes open and effective operations in international trade activities.

17.4 Addressing Challenges in International Payments with Blockchain Technology

Common international payment methods include bank wire transfers (as shown in Figure 17.3), international credit card payments, and third-party payment services, with bank wire transfers being the primary remittance option. These traditional payment settlements operate in a centralised architecture involving multiple intermediary entities. As a result, the payment-clearing process can be cumbersome, 216leading to slow business processing speeds, low payment efficiency, and high costs. Furthermore, the lengthy and complex payment procedures place significant demands on bank personnel, and operational errors can have serious consequences for both parties involved in the trade. The emergence of blockchain technology offers potential solutions to the challenges of traditional international payments. Integrating blockchain into this process makes it possible to eliminate intermediaries, simplify settlement procedures, enhance payment efficiency, and reduce costs, making international payments faster and more cost-effective. Moreover, blockchain reduces risks in operations when performing international payments and protects user privacy.

17.4.1 Payment Efficiency in International Transactions

Payment efficiency mainly refers to processes and the associated time costs. Simplifying these transaction processes and reducing time costs is a very important point for international trade, as it ensures a smooth flow of money and helps reduce foreign exchange risks. Traditional wire transfer systems have multiple steps, such as remitting banks, correspondent banks, payment systems, and receiving banks. Each organisation or institution operates its own independent accounting system, which results in complex procedures such as fund recording, clearing, and reconciliation with the counterparty bank. Subsequently, this structure or framework contains lengthy processing times and low payment efficiency for international transactions. For example, a bank which performs wire transfers for international remittances generally takes 3–5 working days. However, international credit cards or third-party payment services take 3–7 days to process. In the case of large-scale transactions in which a manufacturer purchases raw materials from a supplier, the opportunity cost of waiting several days for payment clearance is significant. These delays can hinder production schedules, impact a company’s ability to fulfil orders, and potentially jeopardise business relationships and financial stability.

Blockchain technology eliminates intermediatory mediators or organisations, reduces payment times in parallel, and maintains proper security. This allows remitters and recipients to make direct P2P payments and settlements. Furthermore, payments can be processed 24/7, regardless of holidays, enabling instant arrivals. In addition, withdrawals are convenient and free of hidden costs.

Stellar (XLM), Ripple (XRP), Corda, and IBM are blockchain platforms used worldwide to create a blockchain-based international payment system. Ripple is a popular platform due to its speed and low transaction costs, which facilitate real-time international transactions. Ripple is a decentralised consensus mechanism that has the ability to perform a transaction in short times to within 3 seconds, significantly improving settlement efficiency (see Figure 17.4).

The efficiency of international payments is of great significance to traders. In a competitive international market, fluctuations in foreign exchange rates significantly impact trading operations. International businesses reduce the exchange rate risk associated with long-term capital occupation while simultaneously accelerating capital turnover, contributing to market prosperity by shortening settlement times.

217

17.4.2 Cost Comparison of International Payment Systems

The traditional international payment system is very complex in India, and transaction costs are also quite high. The Indian banks charge a fee of approximately INR 500 to INR 1,500 for remittance amounts, along with additional charges such as telecommunications fees. For example, SBI or HDFC Bank charges transaction fees based on the remittance amount, which depends on the transaction size and destination. Subsequently, the total cost of each remittance falls in the range of INR 800 to INR 2,000.

Blockchain technology has the potential to significantly simplify the international payment process by reducing payment costs and saving transaction fees for traders. A McKinsey report assesses the introduction of blockchain technology in international payments. It globally decreases transaction costs from nearly $26 per transaction to $15 per transaction, which saves approximately 42% of the amount of both parties involved after the adoption of Ripple blockchain technology in an international payment system. A prominent Indian bank reduced fees from INR 400 per transaction to as low as INR 50. This technology saves users up to 87.5% in fees and greatly minimises payment costs.

Furthermore, a traditional international payment system requires trusted central banks to facilitate payments and settlements between different banks. They are also required to maintain separate margin accounts to minimise transaction risks. Due to the old payment method, a large amount of capital gets stuck for some time, and subsequently, the growth of foreign trade is adversely affected due to the low rate of utilisation of funds. This new method has particularly benefited small and medium-sized enterprises. However, platforms like Ripple eliminate the need for intermediary banks in a blockchain-based international payment system by enabling real-time payments. This approach requires only a single margin account, significantly reducing the amount of capital tied up and enhancing the utilisation rate of funds.

17.4.3 Enhancing Security and Trust in International Transactions

The inherent characteristics of blockchain technology ensure the security, transparency, and reduced risks associated with international payments. Blockchain-based payment methods operate on a push-based model, meaning that when a user sends a payment to a merchant, they do not need to provide their personal information or 218bank account details. Instead, the system uses a secure hash function to transmit a hashed value of the encrypted personal information to the merchant. Due to the one-way nature of the hash function, personal information remains protected and is not leaked. Furthermore, Ripple employs anonymous transactions, which offer additional privacy protection for users.

In contrast, traditional payment systems utilise a centralised pull-based method that requires real-name transactions. To complete a transaction, users must provide their personal information and bank account details to the merchant online. The merchant uses this information to withdraw funds. Consequently, the merchant accumulates many users’ sensitive data, such as bank account numbers and other personal transaction details. This private information is vulnerable to being leaked or sold by the merchant and may also be at risk of theft by criminals, leading to substantial losses for users. Thus, adopting a blockchain-based payment system can enhance user privacy and improve the security of online transactions.

In addition, traditional international payments have significant risks due to relying on commercial credit without guarantees. The importers and exporters themselves must manage trade risks. One of the primary challenges is ensuring that the importer’s payment and the exporter’s shipping information are accurate and reliable. Once the importer remits the funds, they cannot track or control the intermediate links in the payment process, nor do they have visibility into the exporter’s shipping status. The trading parties must rely solely on commercial credit for transactions, which leaves them vulnerable to commercial fraud. Even in the absence of fraud, poor business practices or sudden market changes can create bad faith, exacerbating these risks and leading to significant losses for traders. Such issues can erode trust in international trade and severely hinder its growth.

Blockchain technology can mitigate these trade risks in international payments. Participants in a transaction do not require the endorsement of intermediary institutions. Instead, they upload the transaction contract information to the blockchain, where all parties involved in the trade jointly maintain the transaction details and verify consistency. If one party does not confirm the transaction information, the transaction is rendered ineffective. The blockchain system facilitates automatic payments once both the importer and exporter validate the transaction information.

The payment process begins with the importer making a prepayment to the exporter per the contract. The exporter then ships the goods via a logistics company. Upon verifying the cargo information, the logistics company uploads the delivery note to the blockchain network. Once the importer confirms the transaction details on the blockchain, the remaining balance is settled. Therefore, blockchain-based international payments can effectively resolve trust crises, reduce payment risks, save time, expedite corporate funds’ return, and promote the rapid and sustainable development of international trade.

17.5 Challenges and Recommendations for Blockchain Implementation

The primary obstacle to implementing blockchain technology in international payment settlements is the inherent limitations of its core technology. Significant challenges still need to be addressed, including energy consumption, credit issues, 219security of encryption algorithms, block capacity, and lengthy transaction confirmation times. These technical hurdles impede the broader adoption of blockchain solutions. As a major trading nation, our country must enhance its efforts in independent research and development of blockchain core technology. Financial technology companies should particularly focus on the research outcomes of related domestic and international industries, investing more human and financial resources to actively develop key technologies and business models for blockchain in international payments. This proactive approach will enable us to establish technical reserves and position ourselves as leaders in the technology era.

The decentralised nature of blockchain presents a stark contrast to the current centralised financial model. Consequently, we incorporate blockchain technology into the international payment system, and it is crucial to establish a corresponding regulatory framework. As we know, no single country or institution independently regulates blockchain technology. Therefore, all financial institutions and regulatory authorities worldwide must collaborate together to formulate a blockchain regulatory strategy that suits global trade settlements. This technology ought to balance supervision, innovation, and practical application.

In order to establish a blockchain-based international payments system, we need to benefit from the UK-based regulatory sandbox mechanism. It allows pilot projects to be run across various sectors. For example, selecting blockchain for the transaction settlement banks within free trade zones for trial runs could provide valuable information. This approach enables researchers or developers to refine technology and regulatory policies before rolling out their larger-scale implementations.

Blockchain technology is inherently multidisciplinary, which requires expertise in mathematics, computer science, cybersecurity, communications engineering, and finance. Nevertheless, India presently requires more high-end talent with this composite skill set. To address this gap, leading universities in India are introducing specialised blockchain courses within their mathematics, computer science, or cybersecurity programs. It is recommended that reputable domestic and international blockchain experts from different organisations be engaged to support talent development. In addition, working together with financial technology companies helps prepare blockchain experts for international business transactions.

In addition, it is necessary to establish a uniform system in industry guidelines for implementing blockchain technology in international trade transactions.

The establishment of these standards fosters healthy competition among enterprises, which improves customer satisfaction. It enhances the effectiveness of financial markets and mitigates potential application risks. In addition, uniform industry standards are necessary to monitor the market and formulate better policies. For this, countries and financial institutions should agree on basic aspects such as blockchain terminology, coding, technical development, and standardisation of products and services.

17.6 Conclusion

A blockchain has the potential to enhance processing and reduce inefficiencies in international payments. Blockchain exists as a trusted and decentralised system free of intermediaries. The result is that the costs of transactions, processing time, and the security of financial transactions are also reduced. Blockchain uses cryptography to 220protect user’s privacy and turn to reduce the risk of data breaches and fraud. In addition, blockchain is transparent and immutable; therefore, all transactions are secure and trackable. This also increases the trust in international payment systems, which is quite important when considering international trade and global e-commerce, where banks and payment systems must serve fast and secure payments. However, more research, collaboration, and investment are still needed to fully expose the true power of blockchain in international payment systems. The solutions to the problem of scalability and security in the blockchain space must be done in collaboration between governments and other financial institutions and technology companies to cater for global financial needs. It is a technical challenge that necessitates solving for energy efficiency, compliance with regulations, and a willingness to use innovation to push beyond how the blockchain can be used on a wide and global basis in international payments. But, as it turns out, blockchain is not just a technological change. It is a powerful force behind the future of international payments, bringing greater efficiency and security to the world’s financial systems at a lower cost.
